It may not waive the tenant's code remedies, such as repair-and-deduct or ending the lease for certified violations, or say that nothing you do counts as a constructive eviction. Service interruptions can be excused only for government restrictions you did not cause, necessary repairs, or natural causes beyond your control.

title: Criminal Use Voids the Lease
bodyText: If a tenant or occupant uses the premises for prostitution, illegal gaming, illegal keeping or sale of alcohol, illegal keeping, sale or manufacture of controlled substances, illegal keeping of a weapon or listed explosives offenses, you may elect to treat the lease as void. You may then bring an eviction or ask the court for an order to vacate, including a preliminary injunction giving you possession with an execution to be levied forthwith. The court must first give the tenant notice and a hearing with the chance to cross-examine witnesses. Public and assisted housing has added rules.

title: Sober Home Certification
bodyText: Massachusetts has a voluntary training and accreditation program for alcohol and drug free housing, commonly known as sober homes. A home does not need certification to operate or advertise as alcohol and drug free. But state agencies and statewide treatment vendors may refer people only to certified homes. No statute sets special lease terms or eviction rules for these homes, or gives any legal effect to a drug-free lease addendum. Ordinary rules apply, including your right to void a lease when the premises are used to keep or sell illegal drugs.

title: Domestic Violence Proof Documents
bodyText: You may ask for proof of victim status, including the perpetrator's name if known. Any one of three documents is enough: a valid protective order under chapter 209A or 258E; a court or law enforcement record of the act; or a written verification from a qualified third party, such as a police officer, prosecutor, victim-witness advocate, licensed medical or mental health provider, licensed social worker, or sexual assault or domestic violence counselor. A verification names the organization and the date of the act, with the adult victim's statement under penalty of perjury. Keep all proof confidential.

title: Domestic Violence Lock Change
bodyText: If a tenant, co-tenant or adult household member reasonably believes they face an imminent threat of domestic violence, rape, sexual assault or stalking at the premises, they may ask you to change the unit's locks. Within 2 business days, make a good faith effort to change them or give permission to do so, and give the requester a new key within the same period. You may charge no more than the customary local price. To deny a key to a co-occupant perpetrator you need a protective order or court or police record. Obstructing a lock change can cost three months' rent.

title: Domestic Violence Reprisal Protections
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent to an applicant because they ended a tenancy under the domestic violence law or asked for a lock change. In an eviction, it is a defense that you acted in reprisal because a tenant or household member sought a protective order, used the domestic violence lease protections, or reported domestic violence, rape, sexual assault or stalking to police. A notice to quit within six months after that is presumed a reprisal, which you can rebut only by clear and convincing evidence. A good faith action against a remaining tenant is not retaliation.

title: Domestic Violence Termination
bodyText: A tenant or co-tenant may end the tenancy by written notice to you that a household member is a victim of domestic violence, rape, sexual assault or stalking. The notice must come within 3 months of the most recent act, or while a household member is reasonably in fear of imminent serious physical harm. They must move out within 3 months of the notice or it is void. Their rent liability ends 30 days or 1 full rental period after the quitting date, whichever is later. Other co-tenants stay bound. No lease can waive this.

title: Early Termination Rights
bodyText: Massachusetts gives a tenant few statutory ways to end a lease early. A tenant may end it on notice when a household member is a victim of domestic violence, rape, sexual assault or stalking. A tenant may treat the lease as ended, pay only fair value, and move out when certified code violations go unrepaired after written notice. Otherwise your lease controls. You may keep an amount the parties agreed as damages for breach, but not more than the law allows, and the security deposit cannot be used for it.

title: Eminent Domain and Tenants
bodyText: If the property is taken by eminent domain, a tenant using part of it as a home need not leave until four months after written notice of the taking. When a tenant for years and you both suffer damages, the whole award is assessed without splitting and held in trust. The trustee pays you, from the income, the value of the rent the tenant would otherwise have paid, and the balance to the tenant for the rest of the term. No statute says directly whether the tenant's own rent duty ends, so address takings in your lease.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination
bodyText: Massachusetts gives you no statutory right to end a lease because a sudden environmental or public health event, or a government order, makes occupancy impossible or unlawful. Your lease and general contract law govern. This library offers no clause for it; if you want one, write your own term, and it cannot take away rights a tenant has by law. If the board of health condemns the unit, you must provide a non-owner occupant comparable, suitable housing for the period the code sets. A tenancy at will can still be ended by ordinary written notice.

title: No Infirmity Termination Right
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations do not let a tenant end a lease early because they must move to a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility, or because of a tenant's death. Your lease decides. This library offers no early-release clause for these events; if you want one, add your own term. If a tenancy ends early by surrender or by death, rent is apportioned to the date it ends. Disability laws may still require a reasonable accommodation, such as an early release, in some cases; that question is not settled here.

title: Lease Guaranties
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute specific to lease guaranties. A guarantor's promise to answer for the tenant's debt must be in writing and signed by the guarantor or someone they authorized. No statute limits a guarantor to the original term, so whether a guaranty covers renewals or a later tenancy at will depends on its wording. State clearly whether the guaranty continues through renewals, extensions and holdover.

title: Recovering Rent After Termination
bodyText: In an eviction you may claim possession and the rent and use and occupancy owed, and a judgment for possession includes any rent found due. If you leave the rent claim out, you may still sue for it later. Rent is recoverable in contract. When a lease or tenancy at will ends mid-period by surrender, a nonpayment notice to quit or a death, you may recover a proportional part of that period's rent. A tenant at sufferance owes rent for the time they stay. Contract claims generally must be brought within six years.

title: Holdover Liability
bodyText: A tenant who stays after the tenancy ends owes rent for the time they occupy or keep the unit. After a no-fault termination of a tenancy at will, the tenant owes rent at the same rate for any time they stay during the notice period. Massachusetts has no double-rent or other holdover multiplier. Damages you keep for a breach may not exceed what the law allows or an amount the parties agreed. Only a court can remove a holdover tenant; accepting rent after termination may create a new tenancy, a question of case law.

title: Filing Before the Lease Ends
bodyText: If you expect a tenant to hold over, you may start an eviction before a written lease ends, but only if the lease was for at least six months with a specific termination date. You cannot file before the latest date the lease allows either side to give notice of renewal, or earlier than thirty days before the termination date. Notify all defendants by registered mail within twenty-four hours of filing, show substantial grounds that the tenant will stay without right, and attach a signed copy of the lease. No execution may issue before the day after the termination date.

title: Stays After No-Fault Eviction
bodyText: If you end a tenancy without fault of the tenant, other than by a nonpayment notice, the court may stay judgment and execution for up to six months in total. The limit is twelve months if a handicapped person or someone 60 or older lives there. The tenant may show they cannot find similar housing nearby despite reasonable effort and are acting in good faith, or other facts that warrant a stay. They must pay into court all unpaid rent and use and occupancy for the stay period. Lease waivers of these stays are void. Hotels and short rooming-house stays are excluded.

title: Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: Tenants may petition the court to seal eviction records. A no-fault eviction record can be sealed any time after the case ends. A nonpayment case can be sealed four years after it ends if no eviction or tenant claim was brought in the prior four years and the tenant certifies economic hardship. A fault eviction can be sealed after seven years with a clean seven-year record. Cases dismissed or won by the tenant can be sealed any time. You get notice of most petitions and may object within 7 days. Sealed records cannot appear in tenant screening reports.

title: File Notice of Satisfaction
bodyText: If you obtain a judgment or agreement in an eviction case solely for nonpayment of rent, you must file a notice of satisfaction with the court within 14 days after the tenant satisfies it. If you do not, the tenant may petition to have it deemed satisfied. Once it is satisfied, the tenant may petition to seal the case record, and the court will seal it if no party objects within 7 days.

title: No Statewide Just-Cause Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statewide just-cause eviction rule for ordinary private rentals. A fixed-term lease ends on its date, and a tenancy at will can be ended by proper written notice without a stated reason. Exceptions exist: an owner who took title through foreclosure needs just cause, and tenants in some publicly assisted housing are protected for a period after its affordability restrictions end. A no-fault termination also lets the court grant a stay of up to six or twelve months, and a notice soon after protected tenant activity is presumed a reprisal.

title: Leases After Foreclosure
bodyText: When a residential property is foreclosed, a tenant under an unexpired fixed-term lease becomes a tenant at will. A tenancy at will is not ended by the foreclosure, sale or leasing of the property. A tenant whose rent is subsidized under state or federal law keeps the lease, and the foreclosing party must assume it and the subsidy contract. A mortgagee that takes possession before foreclosure, or conveys title after it, must notify all residential tenants within thirty days.

title: Foreclosing Owners Need Just Cause
bodyText: A lender, servicer, institutional mortgagee or Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac that takes title through foreclosure may evict a bona fide tenant only for just cause, or once a binding sale agreement with a bona fide third-party buyer is signed. Within 30 days it must post and deliver its name, address, phone and where to send rent, with a written notice of the tenant's right to a court hearing. Evictions for nonpayment, uncured breach or refusal to renew wait 30 days after that notice. Each illegal eviction carries a fine of at least $5,000.

title: Eviction Case Timeline
bodyText: An eviction (summary process) starts only after the notice to quit period has run. Use the court's required summons and complaint, have it served by an authorized officer between seven and thirty days before a Monday entry day, and file it with the notice to quit and proof of delivery. Either side may appeal within 10 days after judgment, and no execution issues until those 10 days pass. The officer must give 48 hours' written notice before removing anyone, and may not levy before 9 a.m., after 5 p.m., or on weekends or legal holidays.

title: No Exemption Waiver Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute letting a tenant waive, in a lease, the protections that keep property from being seized to pay a judgment, and none expressly barring it. When you collect a judgment, much of a tenant's property is exempt from seizure on execution, including necessary clothing, beds, a stove and refrigerator, household furniture up to $15,000, and money for rent up to $2,500 a month. Do not rely on a lease waiver of these exemptions; whether one is enforceable is not settled.

title: No Landlord Lien on Belongings
bodyText: Massachusetts gives a residential landlord no lien on, and no right to seize, a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent. Recover possession only through the courts, and collect rent through a judgment. Holding a tenant's property or excluding the tenant to force payment risks liability for three months' rent or treble damages. Much household property is exempt from execution anyway. Innholders have a lien on guests' property for unpaid board and lodging, but that rule covers inns, not residential tenancies.

title: Agreed Damages for Breach
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute on liquidated damages in residential leases. The Attorney General's rule bars you from keeping, as damages for a tenant's breach, more than the damages the law allows, "or an amount which the parties have otherwise agreed as to the amount of the damages." So an agreed figure, such as an early-termination charge, is contemplated. Whether a particular figure is an unenforceable penalty turns on case law. You may not take an agreed-damages amount out of the security deposit. A late-payment penalty is barred until rent is 30 days late.

title: No Lockout for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: You may not change the locks or otherwise shut out a tenant who is behind on rent, even if the lease says you may. Massachusetts allows no one to recover possession except through a summary process (eviction) case or another proceeding authorized by law. A tenant removed or excluded without a valid court order may recover possession or end the tenancy, and recover three months' rent or three times the damages, plus costs and attorney's fees. A lease term exempting you from that liability is void. A lockout is also a crime.

title: Never Name Minors in Eviction
bodyText: Do not name any minor as a defendant in a Massachusetts summary process (eviction) case. The statute says the defendants named in the summons and complaint "shall not include any minors," and any minor's name included must be expunged from the court record and the electronic docket. The Housing Court's standing order repeats the rule. The statute does not say what else happens to a case that names a minor. Name the adult tenants and other adult occupants you seek to remove.

title: Notice to Quit for Nonpayment
bodyText: To end a tenancy for unpaid rent, give the tenant a written fourteen days' notice to quit. Under a written lease, the tenant still keeps the tenancy by paying or tendering all rent then due, with interest and costs of suit, on or before the day the answer is due in your eviction case. A tenant at will who has not received a similar notice in the prior twelve months can stop the termination by paying the full rent due within ten days after receiving the notice. A lease term waiving these notices is void.

title: Required Wording for At-Will Notices
bodyText: Every notice ending a tenancy at will for nonpayment of rent must contain this notification: "If you have not received a notice to quit for nonpayment of rent within the last twelve months, you have a right to prevent termination of your tenancy by paying or tendering to your landlord, your landlord's attorney or the person to whom you customarily pay your rent the full amount of rent due within ten days after your receipt of this notice." If it is left out, the notice stays valid, but the tenant may pay up to the answer date.

title: State Form With Nonpayment Notice
bodyText: Every written notice to quit for nonpayment you give a residential tenant must be accompanied by the state form developed by the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities. It documents any repayment agreement and gives information on rental assistance, court rules and eviction restrictions. It must prominently display: "THIS NOTICE TO QUIT IS NOT AN EVICTION. YOU DO NOT NEED TO IMMEDIATELY LEAVE YOUR UNIT. YOU ARE ENTITLED TO A LEGAL PROCEEDING IN WHICH YOU CAN DEFEND AGAINST THE EVICTION. ONLY A COURT ORDER CAN FORCE YOU TO LEAVE YOUR UNIT." The court will not accept your nonpayment case without proof you delivered the form.

title: Notice to Quit Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A residential lease may not waive the notices to quit Massachusetts requires: the fourteen days' notice for nonpayment and the notice ending a tenancy at will. Any term, in any words, with that effect is void. Whether a term that only shortens a notice counts as a waiver is not stated; treat the statutory periods as minimums. Starting an eviction case before the notice period runs out is also an unfair practice. Lease waivers of the court's power to stay a no-fault eviction are void too.

title: Duty to Act on Illegal Use
bodyText: It is a crime to knowingly let your property for prostitution, illegal gaming, illegal alcohol sales or the illegal keeping, sale or manufacture of controlled substances, or to knowingly permit that use. It is also a crime if, after due notice of such use, you fail to take all reasonable measures to remove the occupants as soon as it can lawfully be done. The penalty is a fine of $100 to $1,000, jail of three months to one year, or both. The same uses let you treat the lease as void and seek possession.

title: Nuisance Suits and Building Closure
bodyText: Prosecutors, the Attorney General, police chiefs, or ten legal voters of the city or town may sue to abate a building used for illegal drug or alcohol activity. The court may enjoin you as owner from permitting it and may close the building for one month to one year after repeated convictions or injunctions, but not other occupied units whose occupants were not involved. For prostitution nuisances, closure for a year can follow if you were notified and did not promptly act to end the tenancy. You may reopen early by paying costs and posting a bond.

title: No Owner Move-In Termination Right
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no statewide rule giving you a right to end a lease so you or a relative can move in, and none regulating a lease term that reserves one. A tenancy at will can be ended without fault by written notice: three months, or if rent is paid more often, the rental interval or thirty days, whichever is longer. A fixed-term lease ends at its end date. In a no-fault eviction the court may stay the eviction up to six months, or twelve months for a disabled tenant or one aged sixty or older. Check local rules.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no bond a tenant can give to deliver possession at the end of the term, enforced by a confessed judgment. Any contract term by which a party agrees to confess judgment, or authorizes someone to confess it, is void, and a judgment taken under it must be set aside on the defendant's motion. The only possession bond in the eviction statute is the bond a tenant posts to appeal a judgment for possession; it covers rent and losses during the appeal, and an indigent tenant with a non-frivolous defense can have it waived.

title: Late Delivery of Possession
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule giving a tenant a set remedy when you cannot deliver possession on the start date. The lease and general contract law decide it. One rule applies: the Attorney General treats it as unfair or deceptive to require rent for periods when the tenant was not obligated to occupy and did not in fact occupy the unit, unless the parties agreed otherwise in writing. Write a lease term that suspends rent until possession and lets the tenant cancel and get all money back after a stated delay.

title: Tenant Property After Eviction
bodyText: After you win possession, only a sheriff or constable may remove the tenant and their belongings, after at least forty-eight hours' written notice, and never before 9 a.m., after 5 p.m., or on a weekend or legal holiday. The officer stores the property with a licensed, bonded public warehouse within 20 miles, or a facility the tenant chooses in writing. You pay the cost of moving the property to storage and may recover it from the tenant. The warehouse may sell unclaimed property only after six months, and the tenant gets one free visit to retrieve personal items.

title: Paying After a Nonpayment Judgment
bodyText: After you win a nonpayment eviction, you do not have to accept full payment of the money judgment. But if the judgment is fully paid, together with use and occupancy accrued since judgment, you may not levy the execution for possession. You must return the execution to the court as satisfied, or tell the court so no execution issues. The tenant is then a lawful tenant and can enforce that in court. Earlier, a tenant under a written lease can stop a nonpayment termination by paying all rent due, with interest and costs, by the answer date.

title: Pending Rental Assistance Pauses Eviction
bodyText: In a nonpayment eviction, the court must grant a continuance, and must stay execution, if the tenancy is being ended solely for nonpayment of rent, the nonpayment was due to a financial hardship, and the tenant shows a pending application for emergency rental assistance. The court may not enter judgment or issue an execution until that application is approved or denied. Emergency rental assistance means public-funded programs such as RAFT run by the state housing office, a municipality or a nonprofit on their behalf.

title: Counterclaims and Rent Paid to Court
bodyText: In a nonpayment or no-fault eviction, a tenant may raise condition and other claims as a defense or counterclaim without first paying rent into court. After hearing the case, the court may order the tenant to pay the clerk the fair value of use and occupation, less any award to the tenant, and may spend those funds on repairs. The tenant may also deposit disputed rent voluntarily. If the tenant's award equals or exceeds what you are owed, you do not get possession. If you are owed more, the tenant keeps possession by paying the balance within one week of the court's notice.

title: False Application Statements
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule giving you a special right to end a lease because the tenant lied on the rental application. A lease term making material false statements a breach is a contract matter, and you must still go through a court eviction. One answer is never false: an applicant with a sealed eviction record may answer "no record" to a question about that sealed record. Do not treat that answer as a misrepresentation.

title: No Retaliation Against Tenants
bodyText: You may not threaten or take reprisals against a tenant for reporting a suspected code or housing-law violation to a board of health or other agency, complaining in writing to you or your agent, suing to enforce housing laws, or organizing or joining a tenants' union. The tenant can recover at least one month's and up to three months' rent, or actual damages if greater, plus costs and attorney's fees. Retaliation is also a defense to eviction, and the defense also protects tenants who seek domestic violence protections or report abuse to police. Lease waivers are void.

title: Six-Month Retaliation Presumption
bodyText: If within six months after a tenant's protected activity you send a notice ending the tenancy (other than for nonpayment of rent), raise the rent, or substantially change the terms, the law presumes it is a reprisal. The same applies to an eviction case or notice to quit in that window. Protected activity by someone else on the tenant's behalf, or relating to the building, also starts the clock. You can rebut the presumption only by clear and convincing evidence that you had independent justification and would have acted the same way, at the same time, anyway.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: Massachusetts bans every form of self-help eviction. You may recover possession only through a court case, ending with an execution levied by a sheriff or constable. Do not remove the tenant or their belongings, change locks, remove doors, or wilfully cut off required heat, water, electricity or other services to force a move. An excluded tenant may get back in or end the tenancy and recover three months' rent or three times the damages, plus fees. Wilful utility shutoffs and interference with quiet enjoyment separately cost the greater of actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, and are crimes.

title: Federal Servicemember Rights Extended
bodyText: Massachusetts extends the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, including its lease-termination and eviction protections, to members of the Massachusetts National Guard and state defense force ordered to active duty by the state or under federal Title 32. Guard members of other states living in Massachusetts on such orders are covered too. After sending a written demand at least 30 days before suing (not needed for a counterclaim), a servicemember may recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, and the court may add attorney's fees; a willful or knowing violation, or a bad-faith refusal of the demand, costs the greater of $5,000 or three times the damages. Before a default eviction judgment, you must file an affidavit about the tenant's military service.

title: No Bias Against Service Members
bodyText: Massachusetts fair housing law bars refusing to rent to someone, or giving them different terms, conditions or privileges, because the person is a veteran or a member of the armed forces. It applies to owners, managing agents, brokers and others with the right to rent covered housing. Do not screen out applicants because they may deploy or be transferred.

title: Late Benefit Checks and Eviction
bodyText: If a tenant fell behind because a federal, state or municipal agency failed or delayed in mailing or delivering a subsistence or rental payment, check or voucher (other than a salary payment), the court must continue the eviction hearing at least seven days so the agency can be notified. If all rent due, with interest and costs, is tendered to you within that time, the court treats the tenancy as not terminated. This applies to written leases and tenancies at will. It covers benefit checks such as Social Security and rent vouchers.

title: When Tenants May End Early
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes let a tenant end a lease early in only a few situations. A tenant or co-tenant may end it by written notice within three months after domestic violence, rape, sexual assault or stalking against a household member. A tenant you exclude without a court order may terminate the rental agreement. A tenant facing certified, unrepaired code violations may treat the lease as abrogated, pay only fair value, and move out. Servicemembers have federal rights, extended to state Guard duty. No statute ends a lease for your misrepresentation; that is case law.

title: Voucher Inspections
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule letting you refuse a subsidized tenancy because of the program's inspection, and no statute on a subsidized tenant's refusal of a program inspection. Instead, Massachusetts makes it unlawful for anyone furnishing rental accommodations to discriminate against a tenant receiving housing subsidies or rental assistance, either because of that subsidy or "because of any requirement" of the program. A unit inspection is a program requirement, so refusing a voucher holder over it risks a discrimination claim.

title: When a Lease Term Ends
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statewide good-cause rule for ending or not renewing an ordinary private lease. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date. If the tenant stays, you must still bring a court eviction; a tenant at sufferance owes rent for the time they occupy. For a written lease of at least six months, you may file up to thirty days before the end date if you can show the tenant is likely to stay, but no execution issues until after it. The court may stay a no-fault eviction. Foreclosing owners and some formerly subsidized buildings need just cause.

title: Tenancies at Will
bodyText: In Massachusetts, any tenancy created without a writing signed by the landlord or the landlord's attorney is a tenancy at will, whatever rent period the parties use. Either party may end it with written notice: three months, or if rent is paid more often, the rental interval or thirty days, whichever is longer. Selling, transferring or leasing the building, or a foreclosure, does not end it by operation of law. A rooming-house occupancy of three consecutive months becomes a tenancy at will. After a foreclosure sale, a tenant under an unexpired lease is deemed a tenant at will.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: You may deduct from the deposit a reasonable repair cost for damage caused by the tenant, anyone under the tenant's control, or anyone on the premises with the tenant's consent, but not reasonable wear and tear. A tenant's statutory repair-and-deduct remedy does not cover conditions caused by the tenant, a household member, or a guest or business invitee. In an eviction, a tenant's condition counterclaim fails if you show the tenant or someone under their control caused it, and a lease waiver of that counterclaim is void. Massachusetts has no casualty-termination statute.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule ending a lease when a tenant dies, letting a tenant name a contact for their property or deposit, or setting a removal procedure for a deceased tenant's belongings. If a written lease or a tenancy at will ends by the death of a party mid-period, rent is apportioned to the date it ended. Whether a written lease ends at the tenant's death is case law. This library offers no clause naming a contact for a tenant's death; if you want one, add your own term. A surviving spouse, parent or child who lived there lawfully may ask the court to stay a no-fault eviction. Check the unit for animals.

title: Notice to End a Tenancy at Will
bodyText: Either you or the tenant may end a tenancy at will, including month-to-month and week-to-week tenancies, by written notice of three months, or, if rent is payable more often than every three months, a notice equal to the rental interval or thirty days, whichever is longer. A week-to-week tenancy therefore needs thirty days. Your notice may offer a new tenancy on different terms. After a no-fault termination you cannot sue for possession until that period has run from the tenant's receipt of written notice. A fixed-term lease needs no statutory notice to end on its date. A lease cannot waive these notices.

title: Ending a Rooming House Occupancy
bodyText: Rooming-house occupancies follow special rules. After more than thirty consecutive days but less than three months, the operator may end an occupancy by seven days' written notice; fraternity, sorority and dormitory rooms follow that rule for any length of stay. Three consecutive months of occupancy creates a tenancy at will. Even then, if rent is payable daily or weekly, seven days' written notice ends it where the occupant is causing a nuisance, substantial damage or substantial interference, and the notice must specify the problem. For a no-fault end with daily or weekly rent, you may sue seven days after written notice.

title: Removing People Who Never Were Tenants
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no special squatter-removal procedure. The general trespass law applies: a person who enters or remains in a dwelling without right after being forbidden by the person in lawful control may be fined, jailed up to thirty days, and arrested by police. That law does not apply to tenants or occupants who rightfully entered at the start of their tenancy or occupancy and stay after it ends or is said to end; you may remove them only through civil court proceedings. When in doubt, treat a long-term occupant as needing an eviction case.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit
bodyText: Massachusetts zoning law says no city or town may prohibit, unreasonably restrict, or require a special permit for one accessory dwelling unit, or its rental, in a single-family zoning district. Towns may still apply reasonable rules such as site plan review, setbacks and height limits, and may restrict or ban short-term rentals of it. A town may not require you to live in either the unit or the main house. A qualifying unit is self-contained with its own entrance and no larger than half the main house or 900 square feet, whichever is smaller. A second unit needs a special permit.

title: No Agreed Actual-Notice Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no landlord-tenant rule that requires "actual notice" or lets the parties add their own method, such as a text message, for statutory notices. The notice statutes mostly just require notice in writing. Electronic delivery of ordinary lease notices works only if both parties agreed to deal electronically, but the electronic transactions law does not apply to eviction, default or right-to-cure notices under a rental agreement for a primary residence. Deliver those on paper.

title: Foreclosure Notices to Tenants
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule requiring you to tell tenants or applicants about a pending foreclosure or other claim against the property. Notice duties arise after the fact. A mortgagee that takes possession or conveys title must notify all residential tenants within thirty days. A foreclosing owner must, within thirty days, post and deliver its name, address, phone number, manager and rent address, and may evict only for just cause. A tenant's unexpired lease becomes a tenancy at will on foreclosure, but a subsidized tenant's lease and subsidy contract are assumed.

title: Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText: Massachusetts has no landlord-tenant statute on automatic renewal clauses, but the Attorney General's fee rule, in force since September 2, 2025, treats an automatic renewal as a "Negative Option Feature" and expressly covers dwelling units for rent. If your lease renews unless the tenant cancels, disclose clearly, conspicuously and in writing before signing that charges will recur and how to cancel; give a simple cancellation method; and for renewals longer than 31 days, send written notice 5 to 30 days before the cancellation deadline. For renewals of 31 days or less, such as month to month, written notice is also required: either that advance notice or a notice at least as often as you charge, showing the amount charged and how to cancel. Whether this reaches every lease renewal is untested.

title: Other Rules Massachusetts Lacks
bodyText: Three protections found in some other states do not exist in Massachusetts statutes or regulations. (1) No ban on letting the same room or unit to two tenants at once, and no statutory remedy for it; general contract and consumer-protection law applies. (2) No rule making smoke-alarm compliance inadmissible in an injury case or barring insurers from reducing payment over it. (3) No special right to end a lease for a false rental application. By contrast, Massachusetts does ban card surcharges in sales transactions; whether that reaches rent is unsettled.

title: Squatters and Other Questions Outside the Landlord-Tenant Law
bodyText: (1) No squatter-specific removal procedure; general trespass law reaches only people who never rightfully entered. (2) No duty to give a receipt for ordinary monthly rent, even in cash; receipts are required only for last month's rent and the security deposit. (3) No statewide rule that a rental registration or license is a precondition to winning possession. But an out-of-state corporation that owns or leases real estate here is transacting business, as is an out-of-state LLC by the same test, and until it files its certificate or registration with the Secretary of the Commonwealth it may not maintain a court case, an eviction included (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 156D, §§ 15.01(b)(1) and 15.02(a); ch. 156C, §§ 48 and 54(a)). Renting under a name other than your own also requires a business certificate filed with the city or town clerk, with a fine of up to $300 for each month of violation, though that statute sets no bar on suing (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 110, § 5). Cities may have their own registration rules.

title: No Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule letting tenants house people displaced by a disaster despite lease guest or occupancy limits, and none limiting such stays or saying when a displaced guest becomes a tenant. Your ordinary guest and occupancy terms apply, subject to fair housing law and the sanitary code. Separately, a fire insurance policy on a multi-unit rental must carry a relocation benefit for tenants displaced by fire. Consider flexibility for displaced family members after a declared emergency.

title: Domestic Violence Citations Check
bodyText: Massachusetts has not moved its protection-order laws: abuse prevention orders remain in chapter 209A and harassment prevention orders in chapter 258E, which the tenant-protection statutes still cite. A 2024 law added "coercive control" to chapter 209A's definition of abuse, but the lease-termination and lock-change statutes use their own, narrower definition of domestic violence, so quote that one in leases. One stale cross-reference: the lease statutes define "owner" by citing a sanitary-code section that the 2023 revision renumbered; the definition now sits in the code's general definitions section.

title: Signing Leases Electronically
bodyText: Massachusetts has adopted the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act. If both parties agree to do business electronically, an electronic signature satisfies a law requiring a signature, and an electronic record satisfies a law requiring a writing, so a lease may be signed electronically. A tenant who agreed to one electronic transaction may refuse others, and that right cannot be waived. The act does not cover notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for a primary residence, so serve notices to quit on paper.

title: Tenants Who Call Police
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no general rule guaranteeing a tenant's right to call police or emergency services or voiding lease terms that penalize such calls. Massachusetts does protect domestic violence reports: evicting a tenant for reporting domestic violence, rape, sexual assault or stalking against a household member to police, or for seeking a protection order, is a defense to eviction, and action within six months is presumed retaliatory. Do not write lease terms that penalize calls for help.

title: No Pre-Suit Dispute Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule authorizing or regulating lease clauses that require informal resolution or mediation before going to court. A written agreement to arbitrate future disputes is generally valid under the state arbitration act. But a lease term waiving the tenant's right to a jury trial is void, and so is a waiver of the tenant's right to raise defenses and counterclaims in an eviction. Keep eviction cases out of any such clause, and do not use it to delay a tenant's statutory remedies. Courts already use pre-trial mediation in eviction cases.

title: Landlord Insurance Rules
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule requiring residential landlords to carry liability insurance, except that short-term rental operators must carry it unless the booking platform does. Two insurance rules do apply. Within fifteen days of a tenant's or official's written request, you must disclose in writing the company insuring the property against fire, the amount of coverage, and who would be paid for a loss; the fine is up to $500. If you own multi-unit property, its fire policy carries a tenant relocation benefit, and you must tell each tenant in writing about that benefit at the start of the tenancy. Lease waivers of either rule are void.

title: Registration and Licensing
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no statewide registration or license for ordinary residential rentals, and no rule making a rental registration a condition of eviction. Two kinds of rentals do need state-law licenses. A lodging house, where lodgings are let to four or more people outside the operator's close family, needs a local license; operating without one can bring a fine of $100 to $500 or jail. A short-term rental operator needs a state certificate of registration, must carry at least $1,000,000 of liability insurance unless the booking platform does, and may face local licensing. Many cities add their own rules. Two general business filings also apply. An out-of-state corporation or LLC that owns or leases real estate here must, within 10 days, file with the Secretary of the Commonwealth, naming an agent in Massachusetts, and cannot maintain an eviction or other court case until it does (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 156D, §§ 15.01(b)(1), 15.02(a) and 15.03; ch. 156C, §§ 48 and 54(a); see "Absentee and Out-of-State Owners"). And anyone renting under a name other than their own must file a business certificate with the city or town clerk, renewed every four years, or face a fine of up to $300 a month (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 110, § 5).

title: No Crime-Free Lease Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule requiring or regulating crime-free lease addenda, and no duty to give police or child-protection investigators information about tenants. The rules that do apply limit what such terms can do. You may treat a lease as void when a tenant uses the unit for listed illegal purposes such as drug dealing, and after notice of such use you must take reasonable lawful steps to remove the occupants. Evicting a tenant for reporting domestic violence to police is a defense to eviction. Eviction still requires a court case. Two general reporting duties do reach you and your staff. Whoever knows that another person is a victim of aggravated rape, rape, murder, manslaughter or armed robbery and is at the scene must report it to law enforcement as soon as reasonably practicable, if it can be done without danger, or face a fine of $500 to $2,500 (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 268, § 40). And any person who knows of a death from violence, accident, suicide or another listed circumstance, including any person found dead, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, must immediately notify the office of the chief medical examiner; the statute's fine for failing applies only to listed professionals (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 38, § 3). Child-abuse and elder-abuse reporting is mandatory only for listed professionals, though anyone may report an older adult's abuse (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 119, § 51A(a); ch. 19A, § 15).

title: No Blank-Space Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule that every blank in a lease must be filled in, or that a blank is a breach. But certain items must appear. The Attorney General treats it as unfair or deceptive to sign a written rental agreement that fails to state fully and conspicuously the owner's and any manager's names, addresses and phone numbers, the person authorized to receive notices and accept service of process, and the deposit amount with the tenant's deposit rights. Fill those in before anyone signs.

title: Give the Tenant a Signed Copy
bodyText: Within thirty days after the tenant signs a written lease or rental agreement, give the tenant a copy signed by you; failing to do so is an unfair or deceptive practice under the Attorney General's rules, which exposes you to consumer-protection claims. Where you agreed orally to sign a lease and got the tenant's signature, a separate statute also imposes a fine of up to $300 for missing that deadline, and a lease waiver of it is void. Neither rule says that a late copy makes the lease unenforceable.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule requiring a tenant to initial a lease term, such as a notice period longer than the law requires, for it to bind the tenant. The statutory notice to end a tenancy at will runs both ways, and Massachusetts says nothing about lengthening it by agreement. A lease cannot shorten or waive the statutory notices. Initials remain good practice for unusual terms.

title: Lease Length and Signatures
bodyText: Massachusetts sets no maximum lease term, but how a lease is made limits it. Any tenancy created without a writing signed by you or your attorney is only a tenancy at will, whatever term the parties intended. A lease for more than seven years binds buyers and lenders without actual notice of it only if the lease or a notice of lease is recorded at the registry of deeds. A lease of 100 years or more is treated like ownership while 50 years remain. Get every lease signed by all parties.

title: Absentee and Out-of-State Owners
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule requiring an out-of-state individual owner to appoint an in-state agent or broker, and none requiring tenants to withhold tax from rent paid to a nonresident. An out-of-state company is different. Owning or leasing real estate in Massachusetts counts as transacting business, so within 10 days an out-of-state corporation must file a certificate with the Secretary of the Commonwealth naming a registered agent in Massachusetts, and an out-of-state LLC must register naming a resident agent. Until it does, it cannot maintain an eviction or any other court case, it owes fees and penalties (for an LLC, a fine of up to $500 a year), and it is treated as having appointed the Secretary as its agent for service of process, though its leases stay valid (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 156D, §§ 15.01(b)(1), 15.02, 15.03 and 15.10(b); ch. 156C, §§ 48 and 54). Whoever you are, having an interest in Massachusetts real property lets a Massachusetts court hear a claim arising from it (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 223A, § 3(e)). Absentee owners still have contact duties. If you do not live in the building, post a notice of at least twenty square inches near the mailboxes or inside with your name, address and phone number, plus any non-resident manager's. A separate statute fines an owner without a resident manager up to $50 a day for not posting. Your written lease must also name the person authorized to accept service of process for you.

title: Delivering Notices
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes require notices to quit to be in writing but do not say how they must be delivered or who may deliver them. Use a method you can prove, such as hand delivery by a constable or certified and first-class mail. Electronic delivery does not count for eviction, default or cure notices on a primary residence. You must accept notices from tenants sent to the address where rent is customarily sent, given to the person who customarily accepts for you, or sent to the person your lease names to receive notices.

title: Extra Terms in Quit Notices
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no required warning for a move-out notice form that adds terms not in the lease. One related rule helps you: a written notice ending a tenancy at will may include an offer of a new tenancy on different terms, and the offer does not make the notice invalid. Keep a nonpayment notice to quit to the facts, include the required wording for tenants at will, and attach the state form. Do not bury new obligations in a document the tenant signs to give notice.

title: Where Your Lease Decides
bodyText: Several Massachusetts rules depend on what a written lease says, and a silent lease takes the default against you. You pay for electricity and gas unless the unit has its own meter and a written rental agreement makes the tenant pay; heating oil works the same way with a separate tank. You supply the stove and refrigerator unless the written agreement requires the tenant to. The tenant clears snow and ice from exits in their exclusive control only if the written agreement clearly says so. Separate water charges, tax escalation and automatic rent increases each need specific written terms. A landlord attorney-fee clause automatically becomes mutual.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no general plain-language or readability law for residential leases, and no required statement listing the tenant's waivers or consumer restrictions. Narrower rules apply. A written rental agreement must state the owner and manager contacts, the person who accepts service, and the deposit amount and the tenant's deposit rights fully and conspicuously, in simple and readily understandable language. A water submetering arrangement must be disclosed in plain language. Automatic rent increase conditions must be stated clearly and conspicuously.

title: Small Landlords and Building Size
bodyText: Most Massachusetts landlord-tenant duties do not change with how many units you own, though fair housing coverage and who pays for disability modifications can turn on owning ten or more units on contiguous land. Some rules turn on the building instead. Most of the fair housing law does not apply to leasing one unit of a two-family house when you live in the other unit, but the ban on discriminating against tenants who receive public assistance or a housing subsidy still applies. If the home is publicly assisted housing, the other fair housing bans apply too, except the rule on families with children, which keeps its own two-family exemption. The duty to fix unsafe conditions after a tenant's certified-mail notice does not apply to owner-occupied two- or three-family homes. In a single-unit building the tenant handles pests and pays for trash collection; with two or more units you do. Multi-unit fire policies carry a tenant relocation benefit. A lodging house with four or more unrelated lodgers needs a license.

title: Code Duties Follow Control
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule saying that a lease, assignment, deed or mortgage cannot let someone collect rent free of habitability duties. The sanitary code reaches the same people another way: "owner" includes anyone with legal title, anyone with care, charge or control of the residence in any capacity, including an agent or trustee, a mortgagee in possession, and a court-appointed receiver. A lease term waiving the tenant's statutory condition remedies is void.

title: Requiring Renters Insurance
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule that permits, bars or limits a lease requirement that the tenant carry renters insurance, and no required notice that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings. Requiring a policy the tenant buys directly from an insurer is not addressed. But at or before move-in you may collect only first and last month's rent, a deposit and a lock and key cost, so do not charge a premium, enrollment or administrative fee then. Renters policies may exclude claims from short-term rentals by the tenant.

title: When the Building Changes Hands
bodyText: Selling, transferring or leasing the building does not end a tenancy at will, and a buyer takes subject to it. A new owner who receives security deposits must, within forty-five days, tell each tenant in writing that it holds the deposit, with its name, business address and phone number and its agent's. The new owner is liable for deposits even if the seller never transferred them. Absentee owners must update the posted contact notice near the mailboxes, including any new manager. After a foreclosure, separate notice and just-cause rules apply to the foreclosing owner.

title: Prescribed Texts and Forms
bodyText: Massachusetts prescribes exact wording for several landlord documents. Copy each word for word. If you take a security deposit, your statement of condition must carry the statutory notice in twelve-point bold-face type at the top of its first page. A notice ending a tenancy at will for nonpayment must contain the statutory notification of the tenant's right to cure. A nonpayment notice to quit must be accompanied by the state housing office's form. A rental application that asks about prior evictions must include the statutory "no record" statement. For a unit built before 1978, before the rental agreement is signed give the state lead notification materials and certification form, along with a copy of the most recent lead inspection report, letter of interim control, letter of compliance or abatement plan, if any exists. For every unit, give each occupant, or post, the health department's Notice of Occupants' Legal Rights and Responsibilities.

title: Protecting Tenant Personal Information
bodyText: If you keep a tenant's or applicant's name together with a Social Security number, driver's license or state ID number, or a bank account or card number, Massachusetts data-security law applies to you. You must keep a written information security program with administrative, technical and physical safeguards suited to your size. If that information is breached, you must give notice to the Attorney General, the state consumer affairs office and the affected person. Shred or destroy old records holding it; fines run up to $100 per person affected.

title: No Rent Ledger Duty
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes, regulations and court rules contain no duty to give a tenant a rent ledger or payment history, and no rule limiting what you may tell third parties about a tenant. Two record duties do apply. If you hold a security deposit, keep the statutory deposit record and let the tenant inspect it on request during business hours. If you sue for unpaid rent, the court's summary process complaint asks you to itemize the amount claimed or attach a rent ledger, so keep an accurate one.

title: Tenant Insurance Claims
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule on whether you may require a tenant to claim on the tenant's own renters insurance, or may claim on it yourself. Two rules limit the idea. Sanitary code repairs are your job, and a lease cannot waive them. A lease term that has the tenant indemnify you, hold you harmless or release you for your own negligence or misconduct is void. So do not make a tenant's policy pay for repairs or losses that are yours.

title: No Sunsetting Tenant Laws
bodyText: As of October 8, 2026, Massachusetts's core landlord-tenant statutes, including the security deposit, notice, eviction and retaliation laws, have no repeal or expiration date. In those statutes, the only dated changes are amendments already in force, such as the broker-fee and up-front-payment changes effective August 1, 2025. One protection is temporary by design: the federal-shutdown protections apply only during a shutdown and a short period after it. Recheck each year, because the legislature amends these laws often.

title: Changing Tenancy Terms
bodyText: Massachusetts has no separate notice rule for changing lease terms, and no special rule for raising a fee the lease already provides. For a tenancy at will, change any term, not just rent, the same way: give written notice ending the tenancy, three months or, if rent is paid more often, the rental interval or thirty days, whichever is longer, and offer a new tenancy on the new terms. During a fixed-term lease, terms change only as the lease allows. A substantial change in terms within six months after protected tenant activity is presumed retaliatory.

title: No Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no duty to translate a lease, even if you advertise or negotiate in another language, and no minimum type size for the lease itself. The one type-size rule for landlords is the statement of condition, whose statutory notice must appear in twelve-point bold-face type. Translation duties fall on government: board of health orders carry a translated warning, and the state housing office publishes the nonpayment notice form's information in the five most common languages besides English.

title: Assistance Animals Under State Law
bodyText: Massachusetts fair housing law makes it discrimination to refuse a reasonable accommodation in your rules, policies, practices or services that a person with a disability may need to use and enjoy a dwelling. A no-pets rule is such a rule. The law also separately bars discriminating in rental terms because a person has a trained dog guide due to blindness or hearing impairment. The statute does not mention emotional support animals, documentation or pet fees; those points rest on the accommodation duty and federal law. Leasing one unit of a two-family home you live in is exempt from the main rental provision.

title: Pet Deposits and Pet Rent
bodyText: Massachusetts has no pet-fee statute, so the general money rules decide. At or before move-in you may collect only first and last month's rent, one security deposit no larger than the first month's rent, and a lock and key cost. A refundable pet deposit is not a separate category, so treat it as part of that one capped deposit, with all deposit-law duties. After move-in you may not demand a deposit above that cap. Monthly pet rent is not addressed; if charged, collect it like rent, never in advance beyond the current month. Never charge pet fees for an assistance animal.

title: Limits on Pet Rules
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute on pets in private rentals, so you may ban, limit or approve pets in the lease, subject to assistance-animal rules. Three limits apply. A lease may not let you enter to remove a pet; entry is allowed only to inspect, repair or show the unit, by court order, or if the unit appears abandoned. A lease term making the tenant indemnify you for your own negligence is void, so pet indemnities must exclude it. Within 3 days after a unit is vacated, inspect it for abandoned animals and report any to animal control or the police.

title: Dog Guide Access Penalty
bodyText: Massachusetts makes it an offense to deprive a blind, deaf or hearing-impaired, or other physically handicapped person accompanied by a dog guide of the accommodations of a place of public accommodation. The fine is up to three hundred dollars, plus damages to the person harmed. A neighboring section of the same chapter defines a place of public accommodation to include the common halls of buildings and lodging for transient or permanent guests, but whether this offense reaches an ordinary apartment is unsettled. In covered housing, refusing a tenant because of a dog guide is a civil fair housing violation, and so is refusing a reasonable accommodation for another assistance animal that a person with a disability needs.

title: No Animal Misrepresentation Crime
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no law making it an offense to misrepresent a pet as a service or assistance animal, in housing or anywhere else, and no state rule on what documentation you may request. If you doubt a request, handle it through the reasonable accommodation process under fair housing law rather than by accusing the tenant of fraud. Do not charge a fee or penalty for a disputed assistance animal request.

title: Towing From Your Property
bodyText: You may have a vehicle towed from your private way or lot only if its driver was forbidden to park there, either directly or by a posted notice. A tenant's own car can be towed on that basis too. Before any tow without the vehicle owner's consent, notify the police chief, in Boston the police commissioner, usually in writing, with the addresses, plate number and names the statute lists. Towing and storage charges are capped at the state's police-tow rates. A tow that skips these steps must release the car free, and authorizing it carries a fine of up to one hundred dollars.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no tenant right to install electric vehicle charging equipment, and no rules for a tenant's charger in shared parking or at the end of a tenancy. Whether to allow one, and on what terms, is up to you and the lease. This library offers no charger clause; if you allow one, put your terms in your own addendum. Massachusetts does protect unit owners: a condominium or homeowners' association may not prohibit or unreasonably restrict an owner's charger in the owner's own or exclusive-use space. If you own a condominium unit, that right is yours, at your expense, installed by a licensed electrician.

title: No Residential Parking Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule on parking in residential leases. Nothing requires you to provide parking, deliver parking rules before signing, use a set heading, separate parking charges from rent, or limit changes to parking rules or space assignments during the term. Parking is governed by the lease. Two general rules still apply: you may not collect a parking deposit or fee at or before move-in beyond the permitted up-front payments, and towing must follow the private-property towing statute. Check local ordinances.

title: Tenant Storage Spaces
bodyText: Massachusetts's self-service storage law covers facilities that rent storage spaces for occupants to store and remove their own property. Its lien and sale procedure is written for those facility operators, not for a storage locker that comes with an apartment, so do not rely on it to sell a tenant's stored belongings. Massachusetts gives residential landlords no lien on tenant property. Rules for a tenant's storage space, such as banning hazardous materials, come from the lease.

title: Cannabis Rules in Leases
bodyText: Massachusetts lets a property owner prohibit or regulate the consumption, display, production, processing, manufacture or sale of marijuana on property it owns or manages, so you may ban smoking. You can most likely ban home growing too, since growing is a form of production, but the law does not say so in those words. The one limit: a lease may not stop a tenant from consuming marijuana by means other than smoking at home, unless allowing it would make you violate federal law. Without a lease ban, adults 21 or older may grow up to 6 plants in their primary residence, 12 per premises. The medical marijuana statute gives patients no extra housing protection.

title: No Waterbed Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in rentals. Nothing gives a tenant a right to one, and nothing limits a lease term banning them or requiring consent or insurance. The lease governs. If you require the tenant to carry insurance for one, the tenant buys it directly; do not collect a premium or fee at or before move-in.

title: Flags, Signs and Religious Items
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no tenant right to display a flag, political sign or religious item that overrides a lease rule, and no limit on lease rules about displays. Your lease may regulate signs and displays. Fair housing law still applies: you may not discriminate because of religious creed in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, so apply display rules evenly and consider allowing small religious items such as a door-frame mezuzah.

title: No Candidate Access Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule requiring you to let political candidates, campaign workers or voter registration volunteers into a multi-unit building, and no duty to set aside an area for voter information. Access to locked common areas for canvassing is up to you. Tenants themselves may still invite visitors to their own units.

title: Tenant Security Cameras
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule giving tenants a right to install security cameras or video doorbells, or limiting lease rules about them. The lease governs. One caution applies to anyone, landlord or tenant: Massachusetts makes it unlawful to secretly hear or secretly record a conversation with a device unless all parties consent. A camera or doorbell that records audio in hallways or common areas can create risk, so address audio recording in your rules.

title: Tenant Air Conditioners
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no tenant right to install a window or portable air conditioner, and no cooling standard you must meet. Your lease may allow, limit or ban tenant units. If a tenant installs their own air conditioner, the sanitary code makes the occupant responsible for installing it properly and keeping it free of leaks and defects. If you install one, you must keep it in operable condition.

title: Solar Restriction Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts has no tenant plug-in or balcony solar statute. But a general law voids any provision in an instrument relating to the ownership or use of real property that forbids or unreasonably restricts installing or using a solar energy system. That law is written broadly enough that it might reach a lease, though no statute says so, so whether a lease ban on a tenant's solar device is enforceable is unsettled. Rather than an outright ban, use reasonable conditions on placement, safety and removal.

title: Firearms in Rentals
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule that bars or protects a private lease term restricting a tenant's lawful firearms, including firearms kept in vehicles in your parking area. The lease governs, subject to fair housing law. Separate rules let public housing authorities and certain subsidized landlords act against illegal weapon possession; those do not govern private leases.

title: Guest Rules
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule limiting lease terms on guests, setting a guest stay limit, barring guest fees, or giving guests or service providers access rights. The lease governs. Keep in mind that a guest who becomes an occupant cannot be removed without court process, that occupancy may not exceed sanitary code space limits, and that guest rules may not be applied differently because of a protected class, such as the presence of children.

title: Key and Rekeying Charges
bodyText: At or before the start of a tenancy you may charge the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock, and nothing more for keys. Massachusetts sets no rule on charging a tenant who loses or fails to return keys. But the security deposit may be used only for unpaid rent or water charges, tax escalation and damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, so whether rekeying for unreturned keys can come out of the deposit is unsettled. Bill it separately instead. Different rules apply to lock changes for domestic violence victims.

title: House Rules
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute on apartment house rules, so they bind a tenant as part of the rental agreement. A rule may not require anything unlawful; a lease term that violates any law is an unfair or deceptive practice. Changing rules mid-tenancy follows the tenancy type: for a tenancy at will, give a termination notice offering new terms; during a fixed-term lease, change rules only as the lease allows. A substantial change in terms within six months after protected tenant activity is presumed retaliatory.

title: Snow and Ice on Exits
bodyText: In a single-unit home, the tenant must keep all exits free from obstruction. In a multi-unit building, you must keep common exits clear and keep every exterior stairway, fire escape, egress balcony and bridge free of snow and ice. A tenant there is responsible for snow and ice only on exits under the tenant's exclusive use and control, and only if a written rental agreement clearly identifies that duty. Other common exits stay your job, though each tenant must keep the landing, porch or deck next to their unit on a common stairway free of obstructions. Towns may also require sidewalk clearing.

title: Bed Bug Disclosure
bodyText: Massachusetts has no bed-bug-specific disclosure. But you must tell a prospective tenant about any condition in the unit that violates the law if you know of it or could find it by a reasonable inspection, and the sanitary code counts bed bugs as pests. In a building with two or more units, a pest infestation is your code violation. You must also inspect each unit for pests before a new occupancy and keep the results. So disclose a known current infestation, and treat it before move-in.

title: No Occupancy Certificate Disclosure
bodyText: No Massachusetts statute requires you to tell a tenant whether the unit has a certificate of occupancy, or to give the tenant a copy; check the State Building Code as well. Many cities and towns run their own rental inspection or certificate programs, so check local rules before renting.

title: No Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule requiring you to disclose defective or corrosive drywall to a tenant. If drywall causes a condition that violates the sanitary code, the general duty to disclose known code violations to a prospective tenant applies.

title: No Flood Disclosure
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule requiring you to tell a tenant that the property is in a flood zone, has flooded before, or lacks flood insurance. Your insurance disclosure duty is limited to fire insurance information on written request. A known flood-related condition that violates the sanitary code, such as standing water or mold, must still be disclosed to a prospective tenant.

title: Contamination Use Limitations
bodyText: Massachusetts has no general rule requiring you to tell tenants about past contamination. Two hazardous-waste cleanup rules can reach a rental, though. If the property is subject to a recorded Notice of Activity and Use Limitation, that notice must be incorporated in full or by reference into every future lease. And if a required system that protects a building from contamination, such as vapor mitigation, fails for 30 or more consecutive days, you must notify the state environmental agency and the building's non-transient occupants.

title: Renting a Condominium Unit
bodyText: If you rent out a condominium unit, you must comply with the condominium's by-laws, rules and master deed restrictions, and the unit may not be used for a purpose the master deed prohibits. Give the condominium association in writing the names of your tenants and occupants, other than visitors staying less than thirty days. The association may charge you for expenses caused by your tenant's misconduct, as a lien on the unit. No statute requires you to give the tenant the association's documents, but a lease that makes the tenant follow them should attach or identify them.

title: Association Can Collect Rent
bodyText: If you own a condominium unit and fall at least twenty-five days behind on common charges, the condominium association may, after giving you a written notice and a chance to respond, direct your tenant to pay rent to it instead, up to the amount owed. You may not retaliate against a tenant who pays rent to the association, and the retaliation presumption and defense apply. A lease clause waiving these rules is void. Tell tenants in a condominium that this can happen.

title: State Fair Housing Classes
bodyText: Massachusetts fair housing law reaches beyond federal law. Besides race, color, religious creed, national origin, sex and handicap, it protects gender identity, sexual orientation, age, genetic information, ancestry, marital status, veterans and members of the armed forces, families with children, and recipients of public assistance or housing subsidies. You may not refuse to rent, set different terms, or ask about or record these traits. Refusing to rent because a unit has lead paint is also unlawful. Exemptions are narrow: leasing one unit of a two-family home you live in is exempt from some provisions, but buildings for three or more families have no such exemption.

title: Discriminatory Rental Ads
bodyText: Do not make, print or publish any notice, statement or advertisement for renting covered housing that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, national origin, genetic information, ancestry, children, marital status, public assistance recipiency or handicap. The state's owner-occupied two-family exemption is written into the rental provision, not the advertising ban, so whether an exempt owner may advertise a preference under state law is unsettled. Federal fair housing law's small-owner exemptions expressly do not cover advertising, so even an exempt owner may not advertise a preference based on race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin. Treat the advertising ban as applying to every listing you post.

title: Voucher and Subsidy Holders
bodyText: Anyone furnishing rental accommodations may not discriminate against a person who receives public assistance, or a tenant who receives federal, state or local housing subsidies such as rental assistance, because of that status or because of any requirement of the assistance or subsidy program. The text contains no exemption for small or owner-occupied properties. So you may not refuse a voucher holder, or set different terms, because of the voucher or the program's rules. Screen subsidy holders by the same lawful criteria as everyone else.

title: Harassment and Interference
bodyText: Massachusetts fair housing law makes it unlawful for an owner, managing agent, broker, their employees or a condominium association to sexually harass a tenant, prospective tenant or buyer. It is a civil violation under that law, not a crime. It is also unlawful for anyone to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with a person exercising fair housing rights, or with someone for helping another person exercise them.

title: Fair Housing Case Forum
bodyText: If the Massachusetts Commission Against Discrimination finds probable cause on a housing complaint against you, it must notify both sides of their right to have the case decided in court instead of at the commission. Either the complainant or you, as respondent, may elect court by giving written notice within twenty days of receiving that notice. The commission then dismisses its case, and the claim proceeds in court.

title: Renting a Condominium Unit
bodyText: If you rent out a condominium unit, you must designate a person or entity to oversee maintenance and repair of the unit. At the start of any tenancy, tell the tenant and the condominium association in writing that person's name and phone number. Also tell the tenant in writing the name and phone number of the association's designee for common-area maintenance and repair. Give written notice whenever either designee changes. Separately, give the association in writing the names of your tenants and occupants, other than visitors for less than thirty days.

title: Condominium Rules and Tenants
bodyText: As a condominium unit owner you must follow the by-laws, the association's rules and the master deed's restrictions, and no unit may be put to a use the master deed prohibits. The association may charge you for expenses caused by your tenants' misconduct. If your common charges are at least twenty-five days late, the association may, after written notice and a statutory procedure, collect rent directly from your tenant. You may not retaliate against a tenant who pays rent to the association, and a lease waiver of this protection is void. No Massachusetts statute addresses satellite dishes or antennas.

title: Condemned Units and Open Orders
bodyText: A unit the board of health has condemned and placarded as unfit for human habitation may not be lived in again until the board gives written approval and removes the placard. No one but the board may remove or deface the placard. Before renting any unit, you must disclose every condition violating the law that you know of or could find by a reasonable inspection, which includes conditions cited in an open inspection order. If you take a security deposit, your statement of condition must list certified or adjudicated code violations then existing. No rule requires a separate written notice of inspection orders as such.

title: Lead Law Deleading Duty
bodyText: If a child under six lives in a unit built before 1978 that has dangerous levels of lead in paint, plaster or other accessible structural material, you must abate or contain it. You may first get a letter of interim control, which lasts one year and can be renewed once, but full compliance is the goal. A new owner has ninety days. Repainting alone never counts. You are strictly liable for a lead-poisoned child's damages unless a letter of full compliance or interim control is in effect, and even then you must use reasonable care. Willfully ignoring a lead order or notice brings treble damages.

title: No Lead-Based Family Discrimination
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent, or offer worse terms, because a unit has or may have lead paint, because renting would trigger your deleading duties, or because a tenant uses rights under the lead law. Refusing to rent to families with children does not satisfy the lead law. Neither does refusing to renew a lease with, or evicting, a family with children; such an eviction also violates the consumer protection law and the anti-retaliation statute. A person harmed may file a discrimination complaint with the Massachusetts Commission Against Discrimination.

title: Deleading Notice, Delay, Relocation
bodyText: Before deleading an occupied rental unit, give its occupants at least ten calendar days' notice of the start date on the state-approved form, and notify all occupants if work will touch common areas or the exterior. Generally no one may occupy the unit during deleading and until cleanup is approved; pregnant women and children under six may not be there. If no lease has been signed, you may delay the tenancy up to thirty days until you get a letter of compliance or interim control, and the prospective tenant bears living costs meanwhile. You may move a current tenant to a substitute unit on reasonable notice if you pay moving expenses and any higher occupancy charge.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no energy-efficiency or meter conservation charge that you must disclose to new tenants or offset against rent.
