The general utility rules still apply. You pay for electricity or gas unless the unit has its own meter serving only that unit and a written rental agreement makes the tenant pay. Water and sewer may be billed to tenants only under the strict water submetering statute.

title: No Meth Lab Disclosure Law
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no duty to disclose, report or clean up a former methamphetamine lab before renting, and no ban on reoccupying one. The general rule still applies: before a tenancy starts you must disclose any condition in the unit that violates the law if you know of it or could find it by a reasonable inspection. Whether leftover contamination is such a violation depends on the facts.

title: No Military Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no lease disclosure for property near a military installation or inside a military noise or accident-potential zone, and no related right for a tenant to end the lease. Massachusetts does not tie any lease disclosure to distance from a named base.

title: No Mold Disclosure Form
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no mold-specific disclosure form or warning for leases. But the sanitary code requires you to keep buildings watertight and free from excess moisture or the appearance of mold. An inspector who finds moisture or mold will look for sources such as leaks, structural defects and poor ventilation, and no environmental testing is needed to find a violation. A mold condition that violates the code must be disclosed to a prospective tenant if you know of it or could find it by a reasonable inspection.

title: No Ordnance or Demolition Notice
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no lease disclosure for a former military ordnance site nearby or for a pending permit to demolish the unit. Shared utility meters are handled by the payment rules instead of a disclosure. A tenant can be made to pay for electricity or gas only if it runs through a meter serving that unit alone and a written rental agreement says so. Electricity or gas you must pay for may run through meters serving several units. Water submetering has its own strict statute.

title: No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no state fact sheet on pets and eviction that you must give a tenant who has a dog or cat, at signing or later. Other animal rules do apply when a tenancy ends, including checking a vacated unit for abandoned animals and handling animals left behind after an eviction.

title: No Statewide Well Testing Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no statewide duty to test a private well or to give well test results to tenants. You must still provide a supply of potable water sufficient in quantity and pressure for every occupant's ordinary needs. The sanitary code defines potable water as water from a source approved by the Department of Environmental Protection or the board of health. Many local boards of health have their own private well rules.

title: No Property Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no duty to tell tenants what part of their rent goes to property taxes, whether yearly or when rent changes. Taxes matter in two other ways. A lease may make a tenant pay part of a real estate tax increase only through a clause stating the tenant's proportional share, the exact percentage, and a refund of any abatement share; any other tax clause is void. And a tenant who is taxed on the real estate may keep that tax out of the rent unless you agreed otherwise.

title: No Radon Disclosure Law
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no radon disclosure, warning or testing duty for rental housing, at any floor level, and no radon-resistant construction mandate tied to rentals. The only radon references concern what home inspectors and licensed inspectors do and drinking water standards. You may choose to test and share results.

title: Recycling and Trash Duties
bodyText: No Massachusetts rule requires you to tell tenants where or how to recycle. But you must provide enough receptacles to store refuse and recyclables before collection, and in buildings with two or more units you pay for final collection and disposal. Tenants must follow their community's rules for separating recyclables, yard waste, food waste and bulk items, and must place refuse in the receptacles you provide. In towns with a Pay As You Throw program, tenants follow its rules and pay all its fees. A tenant may compost in the yard only with your prior written permission.

title: No Rent-Law Coverage Notice
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule requiring a lease or renewal to state whether the unit is covered by a just-cause eviction or rent-increase law. Massachusetts has no such statewide law for private housing. One narrow exception: if you own publicly assisted housing whose affordability restriction will end, you must give all tenants written notice at least two years ahead and a notice of intent at least one year before termination. For three years afterward, a protected low-income tenant's rent may rise only once a year by inflation plus 3 per cent, and eviction requires good cause related to tenant fault.

title: No Sex Offender Notice
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no duty to tell tenants about registered sex offenders living nearby or in the building, and no required registry notice in leases. If you look at registry information, do not use it to commit a crime against an offender or to engage in illegal discrimination or harassment of one. Doing so is punishable by up to two and one-half years in a house of correction, a fine of up to $1,000, or both.

title: No Offender Occupancy Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no statewide rule limiting where registered sex offenders may live, no crime of knowingly leasing a dwelling where two registered offenders live together, and no owner duty tied to an offender's distance from schools or parks. Some cities and towns have adopted their own residency rules.

title: No General Lease Font Rules
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no general font-size or first-page placement rule for leases or lease disclosures. Two specific type rules apply. The statement of condition you give with a security deposit must carry its statutory notice in twelve-point bold-face type at the top of its first page. And if you build the state lead notification and certification form into your lease, you must reproduce it unaltered, without reducing its type size.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no duty to state in a lease, or tell tenants, whether the building has a sprinkler system or when it was last inspected. Where a building has one, do not shut off, disconnect, obstruct or remove any part of it without a written permit from the head of the fire department. Emergency shutoffs for necessary repairs or to prevent freezing are allowed if you notify the fire department immediately and again when it is back in service.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule requiring you to install covers on steam radiators when a tenant asks, and no required radiator-cover lease rider or annual notice. The sanitary code's general heating standards still apply.

title: Psychologically Impacted Property
bodyText: You do not have to tell a tenant that the property is or may be psychologically impacted. That covers a past or present occupant's HIV, AIDS or other illness very unlikely to spread through living in the home; the property having been the site of a felony, suicide or homicide; and alleged supernatural events. A tenant has no claim against you for not disclosing these facts. But you may not lie or make a false statement about them, including in answer to a direct question.

title: No Tenant Purchase Right
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no general right for tenants to buy, or receive an offer on, a rental property you plan to sell, and no statewide rent-cap or just-cause notice for leases. One exception: when a residential building is converted to condominium or cooperative ownership, the 1983 conversion act gives each tenant entitled to its notice a right to buy the unit on terms at least as favorable as those offered to the public (St. 1983, c. 527, § 4(b)); see "Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums". For publicly assisted housing, an owner may not sell before offering the state housing agency the chance to buy, and must notify all tenants in writing of the intent to sell. Tenant notices count as given when handed to the tenant or an adult household member, or mailed first class with a copy left in or under the unit door.

title: Consumer Protection Law for Rentals
bodyText: Massachusetts' consumer protection law bans unfair or deceptive acts in trade or commerce, and the Attorney General's landlord-tenant regulation spells out what that means for rentals. Among other things, it is unfair or deceptive to rent a unit with a violation that may endanger health or safety, to hide known violations, to put any unlawful term in a rental agreement, to leave required owner, notice and deposit information out of a written lease, or to fail to give the tenant a signed copy within thirty days. Whether the law reaches a particular small owner-occupied landlord turns on case law.

title: Consumer Protection Remedies
bodyText: A tenant injured by an unfair or deceptive practice can sue in superior, district or housing court, or raise it as a counterclaim in an eviction. Before filing a separate suit, the tenant must send you a written demand describing the practice and the injury at least thirty days ahead; no demand is needed for a counterclaim. A reasonable written settlement offer made within thirty days of the demand can cap what you owe. Otherwise the tenant recovers actual damages or $25, whichever is greater, two to three times that if the violation was willful or knowing, plus attorney's fees and costs.

title: Liability for Unlawful Lease Terms
bodyText: Putting a term that violates any law into a rental agreement is itself an unfair or deceptive practice, separate from trying to enforce it. The same is true of a penalty clause that does not conform to the security deposit and advance-payment statute, and of a tax escalation clause that does not meet its statute. A tenant injured by such a term may sue under the consumer protection law for actual damages or $25, whichever is greater, two to three times that if the violation was willful or knowing, plus attorney's fees. Review your lease form before using it.

title: No Exculpatory Lease Clauses
bodyText: A lease term, however worded, is void if it makes the tenant indemnify you or hold you harmless, or releases you from liability to the tenant or anyone else, for injury, loss or damage caused by your own omission, fault, negligence or misconduct on the premises or in elevators, stairways, hallways or other appurtenances. You also cannot defend a tenant's injury claim by saying a common-area defect existed when you rented, if it violates the building code when the injury happens, and a lease waiver of that rule is void.

title: No Jury Trial Waiver
bodyText: In a residential lease, a term by which the tenant waives the right to a jury trial in any later litigation with you is void. So is a term saying that nothing you do or fail to do counts as a constructive eviction. Leave both out of Massachusetts leases; including an unlawful term is itself an unfair or deceptive practice.

title: No Confession of Judgment
bodyText: Any lease or other contract term by which the tenant agrees to confess judgment, or authorizes someone else to confess judgment for the tenant, is void, and a judgment by confession taken under it must be set aside on the tenant's motion. A term waiving service of process does not help either: a judgment entered under it will be set aside unless the tenant was served in the usual way, or you sent registered-mail notice at least seven days before entering the case and filed an affidavit saying so.

title: No Lease Unconscionability Statute
bodyText: No Massachusetts statute lets a court strike an unconscionable apartment lease or clause. The commercial code's unconscionability rules cover sales and leases of goods, not housing. Instead, many specific lease terms are void by statute, and the Attorney General's rule makes it unfair or deceptive to include any term that violates the law. Whether the common-law unconscionability doctrine applies to a residential lease term is a case-law question.

title: Lease Terms Massachusetts Voids
bodyText: Leave these out of a Massachusetts lease; each is void. A term that has the tenant indemnify or release you for your own negligence. A jury-trial waiver, or a clause that nothing you do is a constructive eviction. A waiver of the notice-to-quit periods. A right to end the tenancy because the tenant has children. A confession of judgment. A waiver of the tenant's deposit rights, quiet-enjoyment protections, anti-retaliation rights or reciprocal attorney's fees. A tax escalation clause that misses its statutory terms. Late interest or penalties before rent is thirty days late are barred too.

title: No Single Banned-Terms List
bodyText: No single Massachusetts section lists every banned lease term. Prohibitions are spread across the landlord-tenant chapter, the sanitary code, the lead law, condominium law, the Attorney General's rule and general statutes such as the confession-of-judgment ban. The Attorney General's rule works as the catch-all: putting any term that violates any law into a rental agreement is an unfair or deceptive practice. Many statutes add that a lease waiver of their protections is void, including the domestic violence, condominium rent-collection and quiet-enjoyment rules.

title: No Eviction Penalty Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule that specifically voids a lease clause imposing a penalty because of an eviction notice or case. Other limits reach most such clauses. You may not charge interest or a penalty for late rent until it is thirty days overdue. A penalty clause that does not conform to the deposit and advance-payment statute is an unfair or deceptive term. Damages you keep for a breach may not exceed what the law allows or an agreed amount. And if your lease lets you recover attorney's fees, the tenant gets the same right.

title: Notices That Must Be Written
bodyText: Several Massachusetts notices must be in writing, and a lease cannot downgrade them to verbal notice. A fourteen-day notice to quit for nonpayment, under a lease or a tenancy at will, must be given in writing. A tenancy at will ends by written notice of three months, or the rent interval or thirty days if longer. A lease term waiving these notices is void. A tenant ending a tenancy because of domestic violence does so by written notification to you. Use written notices whenever a statute calls for them, even if your lease says otherwise.

title: Families With Children Practices
bodyText: The Massachusetts Commission Against Discrimination treats a child as anyone under 18, and protection for families with children also covers pregnant women and people in the process of getting legal custody of a child. Its examples of unlawful practices include refusing to rent to families with young children because of lead paint, refusing to let families with young children live above a certain floor, and charging families with children higher rent or a higher security deposit. State, local and federal maximum-occupancy limits still apply.

title: Vouchers and Public Assistance
bodyText: You may not discriminate against an applicant or tenant because they receive public assistance or a housing subsidy, such as a rental voucher or rental assistance, or because of any requirement of that assistance or subsidy program. The usual exemption for renting one unit of a two-family home you live in does not apply when the renter receives public assistance or a housing subsidy. Ads, signs and statements may not indicate a preference or limitation based on public assistance. Massachusetts does not require a lease statement about subsidies.

title: No Protected-Trait Inquiries
bodyText: Separate from the ban on refusing to rent, you may not make, or have anyone make, any written or oral inquiry or record about an applicant's race, religious creed, color, national origin, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, age, genetic information, ancestry, marital status, veteran or military status, or handicap, including blindness or hearing impairment. Leave these questions off applications and screening notes. The inquiry ban does not list children or public assistance, but refusing to rent for those reasons is unlawful. The age protection does not cover minors or qualifying senior housing.

title: Immigration Status Questions
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no rule that specifically bars, or requires, asking about an applicant's immigration or citizenship status, and no law making it unlawful to rent to someone who is not lawfully present. National origin and ancestry are protected: you may not refuse to rent, offer worse terms, or make any written or oral inquiry or record concerning an applicant's national origin or ancestry. Whether immigration-status questions amount to national-origin discrimination is a case-law question.

title: Criminal Record Screening Limits
bodyText: You may request standard-access criminal records (CORI) to evaluate an applicant for market-rate housing, but only as the final step in the application, after the applicant signs a CORI Acknowledgment Form. Standard access shows felony convictions for 10 years, misdemeanor convictions for 5 years, and pending charges; older convictions stay visible while a later one is. Do not use standard access to screen other household members. Use CORI only to decide whether to rent, do not pass it on except as the rules allow, and keep it no longer than seven years after the later of the tenancy's end or your decision.

title: Criminal History Denial Steps
bodyText: Before you question an applicant about criminal history, give them a copy of any criminal record you have, from any source, and tell them its source. Before denying an application because of criminal history, notify the applicant, give them the record and its source, give your CORI policy if you have one, identify the information behind the decision, let them dispute its accuracy, give the state's information on correcting a record, and document each step. If a consumer reporting agency supplied it, also give the federal pre-adverse action disclosure. If you run five or more background checks a year, keep a written CORI policy.

title: Keep Domestic Violence Proof Private
bodyText: If you obtain written proof that a household member is a victim of domestic violence, rape, sexual assault or stalking, keep the documents and the information in them confidential. Do not provide them, or allow access to them, to any other person or agency unless the victim gives written authorization, or a court order, government regulation or governmental audit requirement calls for it. Limit who in your office can see them. You also may not refuse to rent to an applicant because they ended an earlier tenancy or asked for a lock change under these protections.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: No general Massachusetts rule bars you from making a tenant reimburse a government fine, but one specific rule does. If you own a large building that must report energy use to the state, a penalty for failing to report may not be assessed on or passed through to a tenant whose unit is less than 5 per cent of the building's gross floor area. Any other fine reimbursement must rest on the lease, may not exceed the damages the law allows or the agreed amount, and may not come out of the security deposit.

title: No Foreign Ownership Limits
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no restriction on foreign nationals, foreign governments or so-called foreign adversaries owning or leasing land, and no lease-length carve-out. Massachusetts law says the opposite: aliens may take, hold, transmit and convey real property, and no title is invalid because a former owner was an alien. Residential tenancies are not limited by a tenant's citizenship.

title: Hot Water Temperature Range
bodyText: You must provide and maintain facilities that heat and deliver hot water in enough quantity and pressure for ordinary use. At fixtures other than a bathtub or shower, hot water must be between 110 and 130 degrees Fahrenheit. At a bathtub or shower, it must be between 110 and 120 degrees. Massachusetts has no separate rule to reset a water heater before each new tenant, but the range applies at all times. An inspector checks how the system actually performs, if possible at the times the tenant says it falls short.

title: No Window Guard Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no requirement to install window guards or window stops where children live, and no required window-guard notice or lease rider. The sanitary code's general window, screen and lock requirements still apply. Some cities may have their own rules.

title: Sprinkler Requirements
bodyText: Every building more than seventy feet tall must have automatic sprinklers under the state building code, including older high-rises built before 1975, except condominium buildings begun before then. In cities and towns that have accepted the local-option laws, every lodging or boarding house letting to six or more unrelated people must be sprinklered, and any building newly built or substantially rehabilitated with four or more dwelling units must have sprinklers. The sprinkler rule for buildings over 7,500 square feet does not apply to residential buildings. Never disable a system without the fire chief's written permit.

title: Why the Library Has No Arbitration Clause for Massachusetts
bodyText: Massachusetts's arbitration act makes a provision in a written contract to arbitrate later disputes valid, enforceable and irrevocable except on grounds that would undo any contract (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 251, § 1). But a residential lease term by which the tenant agrees to waive the right to a jury trial in any later litigation with you is against public policy and void (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15F), and an arbitration clause takes the disputes it covers away from a jury. Putting an unlawful term in a rental agreement is also treated as an unfair or deceptive practice under the Attorney General's consumer protection rules. A tenant injured by one can recover actual damages or $25, whichever is greater, two to three times that if the violation was willful or knowing, plus attorney's fees (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A, § 9(3), (4)), and the Attorney General can seek civil penalties of up to $5,000 per violation (ch. 93A, § 4). Federal law may override the jury rule as applied to arbitration, but a court would decide that only after the lease was in use. Because guessing wrong can mean multiplied damages, this library does not offer an arbitration clause for Massachusetts.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Massachusetts follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Mass. Gen. Laws c. 106, § 3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Mass. Gen. Laws c. 106, § 1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Massachusetts's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Mass. Gen. Laws c. 186 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Massachusetts's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: Abandoned Animals After a Tenant Leaves
bodyText: Massachusetts puts the animal check on the landlord. Not more than 3 days after the owner or landlord knew or should have known that a unit was vacated through termination of the tenancy, abandonment or other removal of the tenant, the owner, landlord or a designee must inspect it for abandoned animals (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 30). An animal found on or in a unit vacated that way counts as abandoned (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 30). The person who finds one must immediately notify an animal control officer, a police officer or another authorized agent of the animal's presence and condition (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 30). A landlord or designee who finds an abandoned animal during this check is not treated as its owner, possessor or the person having charge or custody of it under the animal-cruelty statute (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 30; Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 272, § 77). Failing to inspect or notify carries a civil penalty of up to $500 for a first offense and up to $1,000 for a later one (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 30). Massachusetts has no rule that makes a person who feeds or shelters an animal for a set number of days its owner; the dog laws separately define a 'keeper' as anyone other than the owner who has possession of a dog (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 140, § 136A). The abandoned-animal section does not say what else a landlord may do with the animal, so the cautious course is to hand it to animal control rather than keep it, rehome it or sell it. Put the 3-day check into your move-out routine and keep a note of the inspection and the call.

title: No Professional Cleaning Requirement or Cleaning Fee
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute that lets a landlord require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, and no age-of-carpet test like Colorado's. What controls is the deposit statute. At or before the start of a tenancy a landlord may collect only first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit of up to one month's rent and the cost of a lock and key, so a move-in cleaning fee is not allowed (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)). From the deposit, the landlord may deduct only unpaid rent or water charges, a tax-escalation amount that complies with § 15C, and a reasonable amount to repair damage caused by the tenant or someone under the tenant's control, reasonable wear and tear excluded (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(4)). A damage deduction needs an itemized list sworn under the pains and penalties of perjury, plus written evidence of the cost such as estimates, bills or receipts, within 30 days (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(4)(iii)). No deduction may be made for any other purpose (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(4)). A lease term that conflicts with § 15B is void (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(8)). A landlord who uses such a term and tries to enforce it loses the right to keep any part of the deposit (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(6)(c)). Whether ordinary soiling of a carpet is 'damage' or 'wear and tear' is for case law. The cautious course: don't put a professional-cleaning requirement or a flat cleaning charge in a Massachusetts lease; deduct only for actual damage beyond wear and tear, with the sworn list and receipts.

title: No State Approval Rule for Leasing Tribal or Communal Land
bodyText: Massachusetts has no communal-land system and no state statute requiring a government officer to approve a residential lease of land held by an Indian tribe, as American Samoa and New York do. The state's general lease rules apply: an unwritten lease creates only a tenancy at will, and a lease for more than seven years binds outside buyers and lenders only if it, or a notice of it, is recorded or they have actual notice (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183, §§ 3-4). Land held in trust by the United States for a federally recognized tribe is governed by federal law. If you are asked to lease property on tribal land, get the tribe's and any federal approval requirements in writing before signing.

title: Habitability Protections Massachusetts Tenants Have
bodyText: The habitability protections that several states lack all exist in Massachusetts. The state sanitary code sets statewide 'standards of fitness for human habitation' and has the force of law (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127A). If code violations that may endanger health or safety are certified by the board of health or a court and the owner, after written notice, fails to begin repairs within 5 days and substantially complete them within 14 days, the tenant may make the repairs and deduct the cost from rent, up to four months' rent in a 12-month period, or treat the lease as ended and move out (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127L). In an eviction for nonpayment or a no-fault eviction, the tenant may raise conditions, breach of warranty or violations of law as a defense or counterclaim (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 8A). If the amount the court finds due the tenant equals or exceeds what is due the landlord, there is no recovery of possession (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 8A). Willfully failing to furnish required utilities or services, or interfering with quiet enjoyment, exposes the landlord to actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14). Lease terms waiving these rights are void (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127L; Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 8A; Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14). Treat any code-violation notice as urgent: start repairs within 5 days and finish within 14 unless the board orders sooner.

title: Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums
bodyText: Massachusetts' condominium-conversion act (Acts of 1983, chapter 527) protects tenants when a rental building of four or more units is converted. It does not apply to buildings with fewer than four units, to government-owned housing, or to transient hotel and rooming-house stays of fewer than 14 days (St. 1983, c. 527, § 3). If the building was used for housing within a year before the master deed is recorded, the owner must give each tenant a notice of intent to convert, delivered in person or by certified or registered mail (St. 1983, c. 527, § 4(a)). The notice period is the longer of the tenant's written lease term or one year from the notice (St. 1983, c. 527, § 4(a)). For an elderly (62 or older), handicapped, or low- or moderate-income tenant, it is at least two years (St. 1983, c. 527, § 4(a)). No conversion eviction may be brought before the notice period ends (St. 1983, c. 527, § 4(a)). Each tenant has a right to buy the unit on terms at least as favorable as those offered to the public, exercised by signing a purchase and sale agreement within 90 days after receiving one (St. 1983, c. 527, § 4(b)). A tenant who does not buy and leaves voluntarily on time, with rent paid, gets documented moving costs, capped at $750 ($1,000 for protected tenants) (St. 1983, c. 527, § 4(c)). The owner must help protected tenants find comparable housing in the same city or town, and failing to do so extends the notice period by up to two more years (St. 1983, c. 527, § 4(d)). During the notice period the lease must be extended, with any annual rent increase capped at the lesser of the prior year's CPI increase or 10 percent (St. 1983, c. 527, § 4(e)). Violations are punishable by a fine of at least $1,000 or at least 60 days' imprisonment, per unit (St. 1983, c. 527, § 5). Cities and towns may adopt different conversion rules by a two-thirds vote, and cities with their own special conversion acts are exempt from the state act (St. 1983, c. 527, § 2). Check the current text and any local ordinance before converting. No statute requires a conversion statement in the lease itself, and no Massachusetts statute bars converting rentals to hotel or other transient use.

title: No Electric or Gas Submetering Statute
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute that sets a disclosure or billing regime for a landlord who resells electricity or gas to tenants by submeter, and none that says whether doing so makes the landlord a regulated utility. The utility chapter defines an 'electric company' as a corporation organized for making and selling, transmitting or distributing electricity (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, § 1). Whether a landlord's submeter resale falls under that chapter is for the Department of Public Utilities and case law. Water is different: a landlord may bill submetered water only under a signed written rental agreement that clearly and conspicuously provides for it and fully discloses the arrangement in plain language (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 22(f)). A landlord who bills water under that section is not treated as a water company (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 22(a)). A landlord who shifts responsibility for paying a utility to the occupant without the occupant's knowledge or consent faces the penalties of § 14 (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14). The sanitary code's rule on when an occupant may be made to pay for electricity or gas is in 105 CMR 410, on mass.gov. The cautious course: don't resell electricity or gas by submeter; if the tenant is to pay, put the account in the tenant's name on a meter that serves only the unit, and say so in the lease.

title: No Background-Check Rule for Building Staff
bodyText: Unlike Florida's, Massachusetts statutes and regulations contain no requirement that a landlord or management company run background checks on apartment maintenance staff, managers or other employees. If you do screen employees through the state's criminal offender record information (CORI) system, the CORI statute's rules apply. It is unlawful to request or require a person to provide a copy of his own CORI except as that section authorizes (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 6, § 172(d)). An employer that relies on CORI received from the state, makes its decision within 90 days and follows identity-verification policies is protected from negligent-hiring liability for not doing more (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 6, § 172(e)). Employment screening also runs into state and federal employment laws. Practical guidance: for staff who will hold keys or enter units, a documented screening policy applied the same way to everyone is prudent even though no statute requires it.

title: Large-Building Energy Reporting and Tenant Energy Use
bodyText: Massachusetts requires annual energy reporting for large buildings, those with at least 20,000 square feet of gross floor area (or a lower threshold the Department of Energy Resources sets by regulation) (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 25A, § 20(a)). Each year by June 30 the electric, gas and steam companies report each large building's usage to the department (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 25A, § 20(c)). By the same date the owner must report any other energy the building used (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 25A, § 20(d)). The owner need not report energy ordered, delivered and charged directly to a tenant if it sent the tenant a written request for the information by April 30, got no response by June 25, and gives the department evidence of the request (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 25A, § 20(d)). The department publishes building-by-building results and must use appropriate practices to keep owners' and tenants' personally identifying information from public disclosure (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 25A, § 20(f)). Penalties may not be assessed on or passed through to a tenant whose unit is less than 5 percent of the building's floor area, and they are capped at $150 a day (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 25A, § 20(h)). Boston's and Cambridge's own stricter reporting rules still apply (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 25A, § 20(i)). No statute provides a lease clause authorizing release of a tenant's own utility data, as Vermont's does. If you own a large building where tenants buy energy directly, send the written request by April 30 every year and keep proof.

title: Who May Represent an LLC or Corporation Landlord
bodyText: Only a member in good standing of the Massachusetts bar may practice law, with a lawyer from another state allowed only by the court's permission (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 221, § 46A). The General Laws do not themselves say whether a non-lawyer manager or member may appear for an LLC or corporation in a summary process (eviction) case. The Uniform Summary Process Rules do not answer it either: none of the thirteen rules says who may appear for a party, so the answer lies in case law. Small claims is a separate, informal procedure for money claims up to $7,000, with rules made by the chief justices and approved by the Supreme Judicial Court (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 218, § 21). Those rules have no provision on who may appear for an entity; they let the court limit lawyers' participation and allow non-lawyers to assist a party when that helps the presentation (Uniform Small Claims Rule 7(b)). The cautious course: if your rental is owned by an LLC or corporation, have a Massachusetts attorney file and appear in any eviction. An individual owner may represent himself or herself.

title: No Statute on Tenant EV Chargers at Move-Out
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute on what happens to a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when a tenancy ends. The only installation-rights statute protects condominium and association unit owners, not tenants (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183A, § 10A(b)). Under it, the owner pays for installation, uses a licensed contractor or electrician, and bears the costs of maintenance, repair and replacement until the charger is removed and the common area restored, plus the electricity (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183A, § 10A(c), (e)). Those rules don't bind a landlord and tenant. Treat a tenant's charger as an alteration: agree in writing before installation who owns it, who removes it at move-out, who restores the wall and wiring, and that a licensed electrician does the work. A condominium unit you rent out may also be subject to the association's own EV rules.

title: Rules for Charging Tenants for EV Charging
bodyText: Massachusetts has no tenant right to install an EV charger and no statute on a landlord billing tenants for charging. The weights-and-measures rules for chargers come from the Division of Standards, which must make regulations to inventory charging stations and to ensure accurate pricing and volumes at public charging stations (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 98, § 59(b)). Those regulations do not apply to chargers at residential property with not more than 4 dwelling units (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 98, § 59(c)). A 'public' charging station is one at a publicly available parking space, which excludes spaces reserved for tenants, residents or visitors (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 98, § 59(a)). So a charger reserved for the tenants of a building with 5 or more units may still fall under the inventory rules, but not the public-station pricing rules. The Massachusetts General Laws do not tax electricity sold through a charger or say whether a landlord who resells it becomes an 'electric company' (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, § 1). Building- and energy-code EV-ready requirements for new construction are in regulations on mass.gov. The cautious course for a 5-plus-unit building: check the Division of Standards' charger rules before charging tenants per kilowatt-hour; a flat fee in the lease is simpler.

title: No Rule on Shared EV Chargers in Rentals
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute governing shared EV chargers in a rental building's common parking, and no rule requiring a landlord to provide one or to let tenants install one in a common area. For condominiums and associations, the statute protects only a unit owner's charger in the owner's own or exclusive-use space, and the owner pays for the electricity on the owner's own account where possible (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183A, § 10A(b), (e)). A landlord who installs a shared charger for tenants at a building with 5 or more units should check the Division of Standards' charging-station rules, because the statute excludes from them only property with not more than 4 dwelling units (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 98, § 59(c)). If you offer a shared charger, set the rules (who may use it, time limits, how electricity is paid for) in your house rules or a parking addendum.

title: Who Can Be Served With Eviction Papers
bodyText: The eviction summons and complaint must be served 7 to 30 days before the entry day, and not before the tenancy has ended except as a statute allows (Uniform Summary Process Rule 2(b)). Service follows the Rules of Civil Procedure: by a sheriff, deputy sheriff, special sheriff or other person authorized by law, delivering the papers to the tenant in hand, leaving them at the tenant's last and usual place of abode, or delivering them to an agent authorized by appointment or by statute to receive service; if service is not made in hand, the server must also mail a copy first-class to the tenant (Uniform Summary Process Rule 2(b); Mass. R. Civ. P. 4(c), 4(d)(1)). The rules do not say whether a term in a lease you draft counts as the tenant appointing an agent, so the library offers no such clause: have the tenant served in hand or at the home. The statutes do settle two points. A participant in the state's address confidentiality program designates the Secretary of the Commonwealth as agent for service of process and for receipt of first-class mail (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 9A, § 2(2)(ii)). The 48-hour notice of the levy on an execution for possession must be served in the same manner as the summary process summons and complaint (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 3). If a tenant tells you they are in the address confidentiality program, ask the court clerk how to serve them before filing.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText: Massachusetts lets either the owner or the tenant of private land control hunting on it by posting. A person may not fish, hunt or trap on private land without permission of the owner or tenant after the owner or tenant has conspicuously posted notices bearing the owner's or tenant's name that prohibit it (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 131, § 36). Hunting and fishing licenses must be shown on demand of, among others, the owner or lessee of the land where they are being used (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 131, § 32). No statute decides whether hunting and fishing rights pass to a farm tenant with the lease, as Arkansas's does. So if you rent out land and want to keep or give away hunting rights, say so in the lease, and agree who will post the land.

title: No Pre-Lease Foreclosure Disclosure
bodyText: Massachusetts does not require a landlord to tell a prospective tenant that the property is in foreclosure before signing a lease, and no self-repealed statute on the subject was found. The foreclosure rules that do exist apply after the fact. On a foreclosure sale, a tenant under an unexpired lease becomes a tenant at will, except that a subsidized tenant's lease and subsidy contract are assumed by the foreclosing entity (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 13A). A mortgagee taking possession or conveying title must notify all residential tenants within 30 days (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 244, § 15A). A foreclosing owner may evict only for just cause or after a binding purchase and sale agreement with a bona fide third-party buyer (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 2). Within 30 days it must post and deliver a notice naming who to contact and where to send rent (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 3). Although no disclosure is required, hiding a known foreclosure from an applicant risks a consumer-protection claim, so the cautious course is to tell applicants in writing if a foreclosure is pending.

title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: Massachusetts gives tenants several chances to pay and keep the tenancy. A tenant under a written lease who gets a 14-day notice to quit for nonpayment keeps the lease by paying or tendering all rent due, with interest and costs of suit, on or before the day the answer is due in the eviction case (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 11). A tenant at will may cure within 10 days after receiving the notice, unless the tenant received a similar notice in the prior 12 months (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12). Every at-will nonpayment notice must state that right; if it doesn't, the tenant may pay up to the answer date (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12). A lease term waiving these notices is void (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15A). After judgment for nonpayment, if the money judgment and all use and occupancy since judgment are fully paid, the landlord may not levy on the execution for possession and the tenant becomes a lawful tenant again (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 3). The landlord need not accept that payment, but refusing it doesn't stop enforcement of the money judgment in a lawful way (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 3). Massachusetts has no rule on how a notice must word a landlord's election to forfeit the lease. Use a nonpayment notice that tracks the statutes, and decide before accepting money after judgment whether you mean to restore the tenancy.

title: Codes Fixed to a Named Edition
bodyText: Massachusetts's building code is a state regulation, the State Building Code (780 CMR), written by the Board of Building Regulations and Standards under its statute (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 143, §§ 93-94), and it is fixed to named editions of outside model codes rather than whatever is current. The tenth edition became the only building code in effect on June 30, 2025, and it is based on modified versions of the 2021 International Codes, including the International Building, Residential, Existing Building, Mechanical, Energy Conservation, Swimming Pool and Spa, and Fire Codes (Board of Building Regulations and Standards, tenth edition handbook). So when a Massachusetts rule refers to the building code, read the Massachusetts amendments to the 2021 I-Codes, not the newest ICC edition. The fire code (527 CMR 1.00) is likewise fixed: it is based on the 2021 edition of NFPA 1 with Massachusetts amendments, in effect since December 9, 2022. The accessibility rules (521 CMR) are the Architectural Access Board's own 2006 edition, still in force, and adopt no outside model code. Before relying on any outside standard, check the edition the Massachusetts regulation names.

title: No Good-Cause Coverage Notice
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statewide good-cause eviction law for ordinary private rentals, so there is no notice telling tenants whether such a law covers them. Cities and towns may not enact or enforce rent control of any kind except under the narrow, voluntary terms of chapter 40P (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40P, § 4). The one statewide good-cause rule is for foreclosed homes: a foreclosing owner may evict a tenant only for just cause or after a binding purchase and sale agreement with a bona fide third-party buyer (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 2). A foreclosing owner may not evict for just cause unless it delivered to each tenant, with its 30-day ownership notice, a written disclosure of the tenant's right to a court hearing before eviction (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186A, § 3). Some cities have special acts or ordinances of their own; check local law before relying on a no-cause notice.

title: No Statute on Guest Rights or Guest Fees
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute giving tenants a right to have guests or service providers visit, and none barring a guest fee, as Pennsylvania and New Mexico do. Other rules limit what a guest policy can do. At or before move-in, a landlord may collect only first and last month's rent, a deposit and a lock-and-key charge, so an up-front guest or occupant fee isn't allowed (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)). A landlord who directly or indirectly interferes with a tenant's quiet enjoyment faces damages of at least three months' rent (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14). The criminal trespass statute lets the person in lawful control forbid a non-tenant to enter or remain, but it does not reach tenants or occupants who rightfully entered at the start of their tenancy, who may be removed only by civil proceedings (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 266, § 120). Keep a guest policy to reasonable limits on long stays and conduct, and don't charge for visitors.

title: The Statement of Condition Takes the Place of an Inspection Notice
bodyText: Massachusetts has no rule requiring a landlord to notify the tenant of a right to a move-in or move-out inspection, so there is no penalty for skipping one. The state's version is the statement of condition. A landlord who takes a security deposit must give the tenant, on receiving it or within 10 days after the tenancy starts, whichever is later, a separate signed written statement of the unit's condition listing any existing damage, including certified code violations (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(2)(c)). The statement must carry, in 12-point bold type at the top, the statutory notice telling the tenant to return it within 15 days (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(2)(c)). A deposit may be required only if the tenant is given this statement (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)(iii)). No deduction may be made for damage listed in it or in the tenant's signed list, unless the landlord later repaired it and can prove the new damage is unrelated and tenant-caused (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(4)). The landlord may enter to inspect for deposit damage within the last 30 days of the tenancy or after either side gives notice of termination (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(a)(iii)). Do the statement of condition carefully at every move-in; it is both a legal condition of holding the deposit and your evidence at move-out.

title: Late Fee Limits
bodyText: Massachusetts limits when, not how much. No lease or rental agreement may impose any interest or penalty for failure to pay rent until 30 days after the rent was due (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(c)). A lease term that conflicts with § 15B is void (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(8)). No statute sets a dollar or percentage cap on a residential late fee once that 30-day period has passed. By contrast, the self-storage statute lets an operator charge a reasonable late fee, which it says may be computed as the greater of $20 a month or 20 percent of the monthly rent (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 105A, § 5); there is no dwelling counterpart. Late fees in manufactured housing communities are governed by Attorney General regulations. Write the late-fee clause so nothing is charged before day 31 and keep the amount modest, because an excessive fee may be challenged as a penalty under case law.

title: Lead Law Notice and Tenant Certification
bodyText: Massachusetts has no lead-safe certificate that must be attached to the lease as an exhibit, and no periodic lead-safe registration of rentals. Instead, before entering into a tenancy agreement, the owner must give a prospective tenant the state's lead notification materials and standard form, a copy of the most recent lead inspection report, letter of interim control, letter of compliance or abatement plan for the unit and common areas, and two copies of a statement certifying that the tenant received them, one for each side (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 197A(d)(2)). That certification may be included as a provision in a written lease (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 197A(d)(2)). The owner must also disclose any information actually known about where lead paint or other lead materials are, including covered or encapsulated surfaces (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 197A(d)(1)). An owner who fails to comply is liable for all damages caused and a penalty of up to $1,000 (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 197A(e)). Separately, whenever a child under six lives in a unit with dangerous levels of lead, the owner must abate or contain it (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 197(a)). The federal lead disclosure applies too. The form's own type-size and content rules are in 105 CMR 460, on mass.gov.

title: Recording a Massachusetts Lease
bodyText: Recording an ordinary residential lease in Massachusetts is optional. A lease for more than seven years is not valid against anyone except the landlord, the landlord's heirs and devisees and people with actual notice, unless the lease, an office copy or a 'notice of lease' is recorded in the registry of deeds where the land lies (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183, § 4). A notice of lease must be signed by all parties and state the lease date, a description of the premises, the term with its start date and any extension or renewal rights (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183, § 4). A lease of seven years or less needs no recording to bind a later buyer or lender. Massachusetts has no rule, like Nebraska's, about unrecorded leases to relatives. Recording a lease doesn't change any tenant right under chapter 186. Land registered with the Land Court has its own registration rules.

title: No Minimum Type Size for the Whole Lease
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute setting a minimum type size for a printed residential lease and no rule, like New York's, keeping a small-print lease out of evidence. The one type-size rule in the landlord-tenant chapter is for the statement of condition: its required notice must appear in 12-point bold type at the top of the first page (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(2)(c)). The lead law notification form has its own format rules in regulations on mass.gov. Use a readable size (11 or 12 point) anyway: a lease a tenant can read is easier to enforce.

title: Time Limit to Sue for Rent or Damages
bodyText: Massachusetts' landlord-tenant chapter sets no special deadline for suing a former tenant, so the general limitation periods apply. A suit for unpaid rent or other breach of the lease is an action of contract and must be brought within six years after the claim accrues (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 260, § 2). An action upon a contract under seal may be brought within twenty years (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 260, § 1). Whether a particular lease counts as 'under seal' is for case law, so plan on six years. A claim in tort, such as for property damage not tied to the lease, must be brought within three years (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 260, § 2A). A new promise or acknowledgment of the debt extends the period only if it is in a writing signed by the tenant (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 260, § 13). That writing rule does not alter the effect of a part payment, but the landlord's own note of a payment is not enough proof of it (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 260, § 14). Sue promptly, get any payment plan signed by the tenant, and keep proof of every payment received.

title: Shifting Repairs to the Tenant
bodyText: Massachusetts allows only one statutory way to move repair duties to a tenant by lease. Any lease term that waives the tenant's repair-and-deduct rights is void, except a covenant in a lease of two years' duration, not counting renewal periods, in which the tenant undertakes to make certain defined repairs or renovations in exchange for a substantially lower rent (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127L). The tenant's repair rights are not to be read as imposing a duty to repair on the tenant, or as relieving the landlord of any duty under the sanitary code (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127L). A lease term exempting the landlord from liability for its own negligence is void (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15). The sanitary code lets a written agreement assign some routine occupant duties (such as certain utilities or extermination in a single unit). Don't use a general 'tenant handles all repairs' clause; if you want a tenant to take on defined repairs, use a two-year lease that lists them and shows the rent reduction.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits in Massachusetts
bodyText: Massachusetts needs no separate notice for a nonrefundable deposit because it doesn't allow one. At or before move-in a landlord may collect only first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit of up to the first month's rent and the cost of a lock and key (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)). A security deposit stays the tenant's property (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(e)). It may be reduced only for the deductions the statute lists (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(4)). The one exception is a future 'fee in lieu' of a security deposit, which the state housing office may authorize by regulation. Such a fee may be entirely or partially non-refundable only if the lease discloses that, and the tenant agrees in writing and acknowledges understanding it (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)(iii)). The fee must be optional, capped with any deposit at one month's rent, and offered to every approved applicant (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)(iii)). Don't charge any non-refundable cleaning, pet, move-in or administrative fee.

title: No Statute on Parking Rules in Leases
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute requiring parking or towing rules to be delivered before signing, to carry a set heading, or to stay fixed during the lease, and none limiting what vehicle information a landlord may ask for or requiring the lease to state parking fees. The rule that matters is the towing statute. A vehicle may be towed from private property only if its operator was forbidden to park there, directly or by posted notice, by the person in lawful control of the property (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 266, § 120D). Before any non-consensual tow, that person must notify the police chief (in Boston, the police commissioner) in writing, with the address, the destination, the registration number, the controller's name and the towing company (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 266, § 120D). A tower who did not comply in full must release the vehicle without charge (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 266, § 120D). Massachusetts has no waiting period before towing a resident's car for expired registration. Put your parking rules in the lease or house rules, post the property, and notify police before every tow.

title: Tenant Rights a Massachusetts Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Massachusetts has no single section voiding every waiver of the habitability chapter; instead, each statute carries its own anti-waiver sentence. A lease term is void if it waives: the tenant's repair-and-deduct rights, except the two-year defined-repairs covenant (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127L); the rent-withholding defense and counterclaim (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 8A); the utilities and quiet-enjoyment protections (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14); the landlord's liability for its own negligence (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15); the notices to quit (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15A); the security deposit rules (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(8)); jury trial or constructive eviction, and the remedy for lockouts (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15F); the anti-retaliation rule (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 18); the domestic-violence protections (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 28); and the utility-shutoff notice rights (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, § 124D; Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 165, § 11E). No statute was found voiding a waiver in a sale-and-leaseback of a home in foreclosure, as Missouri's and Oregon's do. Leave these subjects out of the lease, or track the statute's own terms.

title: No Pre-Lease Pest Control Notice
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute requiring a landlord to give a prospective tenant a pest-control or pesticide notice before signing, as California does. The pesticide control act's notification sections cover utilities' rights-of-way and schools and child care centers, not residential rentals (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 132B). Notice to occupants before an indoor pesticide application, and the owner's and occupants' duties during treatment, are set by the state sanitary code and pesticide regulations published on mass.gov. Give tenants advance written notice of any treatment, with the date, the areas and the product, and any preparation instructions.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Massachusetts has no general plain-language law for residential leases, and none requiring a lease to be divided and captioned or to carry a front-page summary of landlord-protective terms. The consumer protection act declares unfair or deceptive acts or practices in trade or commerce unlawful and lets the Attorney General make rules interpreting it (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A, § 2). The Attorney General's landlord-tenant rules under that act are on mass.gov. One statute does require plain language: a landlord may bill submetered water only under a written rental agreement that fully discloses the arrangement in plain language (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 22(f)). Write the lease in short, clear sentences anyway; a term a tenant could not understand is harder to enforce.

title: No Proposition 65-Style Warnings
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 chemical-exposure warnings do not apply in Massachusetts, and Massachusetts has no comparable statute requiring rental-property warnings about chemicals. The state's environmental disclosures for rentals are specific: the lead law notification and tenant certification before a tenancy begins (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 197A(d)(2)), plus the federal lead-based paint disclosure. No general chemical-warning sign or lease notice is required.

title: No Statute on Religious Displays
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute giving tenants a right to display religious or cultural items on their doors or in common areas, as Nevada and Connecticut do. The fair housing law still applies: it is unlawful to discriminate against a person because of religious creed in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(6)(b), (7)(b)). A display rule that falls more heavily on one religion, or is enforced only against some faiths, risks a discrimination claim. If you limit displays, write a neutral rule (for example, about size or damage to doors) and apply it to everyone the same way.

title: Which Fees a Massachusetts Landlord May Charge
bodyText: Massachusetts limits fees mainly by what may be collected up front. At or before the start of a tenancy, a landlord or the landlord's agent may require only first month's rent, last month's rent at the same rate, a security deposit of up to one month's rent and the purchase and installation cost of a lock and key (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)). Since August 1, 2025 that limit also covers amounts paid to the landlord's agent (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)). After the tenancy starts, the landlord may not demand rent in advance beyond the current month or a deposit above the allowed amount (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(d)). Late interest or penalties may not be charged until rent is 30 days overdue (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(c)). A tax-escalation clause is valid only if it states the tenant's proportional share, the exact percentage and the refund of any abatement (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15C). Separate water charges need a signed written rental agreement that clearly provides for them (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 22(f)). No statute requires the lease to list every fee, sets a notice period for adding one, caps third-party billing markups, bans common-area fees or requires a 'total monthly payment' line. The Attorney General's fee-disclosure regulation, which requires the nature, purpose and amount of each fee to be shown with the price, is on mass.gov. List every recurring charge in the lease anyway; a charge the lease doesn't authorize is hard to collect.

title: No State Tenant Guide Required Before Signing
bodyText: Massachusetts does not require a landlord to give a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights before a lease is signed or renewed, with a signed acknowledgment, as Delaware does. The state-prepared materials a landlord must hand out are tied to specific events. Before a tenancy begins, the owner must give the lead law notification and tenant certification forms (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 197A(d)(2)). With any notice to quit for nonpayment, the landlord must include the state housing office's form describing rental assistance, court rules and eviction restrictions, which must state in capitals that the notice to quit is not an eviction (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 31(a)). The court will not accept a nonpayment eviction for filing without proof that form was delivered (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 31(b)). Any fair housing poster or brochure rule is in regulations on mass.gov. Keep current copies of both state forms on file.

title: Seasonal and Vacation Rentals
bodyText: Massachusetts has no separate seasonal-tenancy statute, but it treats short vacation rentals differently. The security deposit and up-front payment rules of § 15B do not apply to any lease, rental, occupancy or tenancy of 100 days or less that is for a vacation or recreational purpose (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(9)). A seasonal lease for a fixed term ends on its own at the end of the term, and a person holding over after that may be removed through summary process (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 1). Other tenant protections, such as the ban on self-help eviction and the quiet-enjoyment statute, still apply to any dwelling other than a hotel room (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14). Short-term rentals are also subject to the state room-occupancy tax regime and local short-term rental rules (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 64G, § 1). Use a written lease with fixed start and end dates and state that the rental is for vacation purposes.

title: Security Deposit Limit
bodyText: A Massachusetts security deposit may not exceed the first month's rent (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)(iii)). The cap is the same for every kind of tenancy, with no extra amount allowed for pets, alterations or risk. A landlord may also collect last month's rent at the same rate as the first, and the cost of a lock and key, but nothing else up front (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)). After the tenancy begins, no landlord or successor may demand a security deposit above the amount the section allows (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(d)). Because the cap is stated as the first month's rent, the cautious reading is that a landlord may not top up the deposit after a later rent increase. The deposit rules do not apply to vacation rentals of 100 days or less (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(9)). A future optional fee in lieu of a deposit, if the state authorizes one, plus any deposit, may not exceed one month's rent in total (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)(iii)). Don't ask for a separate pet deposit or a larger deposit for a riskier applicant.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose shoreline access or public rights of way in a lease, as Rhode Island does. Waterfront property is still subject to public rights under the waterways statute. Private tidelands are held subject to an easement of the public for navigation, free fishing and fowling, and passing freely over and through the water (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 91, § 1). Commonwealth tidelands are held in trust for the public (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 91, § 1). Where those rights reach a particular beach is a fact and case-law question. If you rent waterfront property, don't promise the tenant a 'private beach' unless you know the public has no rights there.

title: Shorter Notice for Showings: No Statutory Period to Waive
bodyText: Massachusetts statutes set no notice period for a landlord's entry to show the unit, so there is no statutory period for a tenant to waive. A lease may allow the landlord to enter only to inspect, to make repairs or to show the unit to a prospective tenant, purchaser, mortgagee or its agents (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(a)). The landlord may also enter under a court order, if the unit appears abandoned, or to inspect for deposit damage in the last 30 days of the tenancy or after notice of termination (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(a)). Entry still must not interfere with the tenant's quiet enjoyment (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14). Any notice rule in the state sanitary code is published on mass.gov. Give reasonable advance notice (24 hours is a common practice) and show at reasonable times; a lease clause allowing showings with no notice invites a quiet-enjoyment claim.

title: Renting in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute limiting rentals of homes in single-family zones to owner-occupied lots. The Zoning Act goes the other way for accessory dwelling units. No zoning ordinance or by-law may prohibit, unreasonably restrict or require a special permit for one accessory dwelling unit, or its rental, in a single-family zone (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40A, § 3). Such a unit may not be made to require owner occupancy of either the accessory unit or the main house (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40A, § 3). Towns may still apply reasonable regulations, such as site plan review, setbacks and septic rules, and may restrict or prohibit short-term rental of the unit (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40A, § 3). More than one accessory unit needs a special permit (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40A, § 3). Massachusetts has no lot-split or two-unit program like California's. Check the town's by-law on short-term rentals before renting an accessory unit for less than a month.

title: Smoke From Other Units and the Smoke-Free Workplace Law
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute on smoke drifting between units, no required smoke disclosure and no rule on a tenant's waiver of smoke-drift complaints. The smoke-free workplace law may reach some apartment common areas. It requires employers to provide a smoke-free environment for employees in an enclosed workplace and bans smoking in workplaces and in places such as elevators, hallways and staircases (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 270, § 22(b)). A 'workplace' is an indoor area where one or more employees perform a service for compensation and the employer has the right to control the space (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 270, § 22(a)). Smoking is permitted in private residences, which include apartments (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 270, § 22(a), (c)(1)). 'Smoking' includes e-cigarettes and other vaping products (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 270, § 22(a)). Whether a building's common hallways are a 'workplace' because staff work there is for case law and Department of Public Health guidance. The cautious course: ban smoking in all enclosed common areas by lease or house rule, and handle drift complaints under the quiet-enjoyment statute rather than asking tenants to waive them.

title: No Special District Statement Required
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute requiring a lease to state whether the property is in a special taxing or improvement district, as Puerto Rico's and some western states' laws do. Municipal charges that can become a lien on the property, such as water and sewer charges and betterments, are the owner's concern; a lease may pass through an increase in real estate taxes only under a tax-escalation clause that meets § 15C (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15C). No disclosure is required, but if a special assessment will be passed on to the tenant, the lease must say so clearly.

title: When a Lease Must Be in Writing
bodyText: In Massachusetts, an estate or interest in land created without a writing signed by the landlord or the landlord's attorney has the force of an estate at will only (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183, § 3). So an oral 'lease' of any length is a tenancy at will. No estate or interest in land may be assigned, granted or surrendered except by such a writing or by operation of law (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183, § 3). The Statute of Frauds also bars suit on a contract concerning an interest in land, or on an agreement not to be performed within one year, unless it or a memorandum of it is in writing and signed by the party to be charged (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 259, § 1). The state's long-lease threshold is a recording rule, not a validity rule: a lease for more than seven years is not valid against third parties without actual notice unless it, or a notice of lease, is recorded (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183, § 4). Put every lease, renewal, assignment and surrender in a signed writing.

title: Massachusetts' Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Massachusetts' main money limits for residential rentals: up front, only first month's rent, last month's rent at the same rate, a security deposit of up to the first month's rent and the cost of a lock and key (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)); no interest or penalty for late rent until 30 days after it is due (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(c)); no advance rent beyond the current month after the tenancy starts (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(d)); interest on a deposit held a year or more, and on last month's rent, at 5 percent or the lesser rate the bank pays (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(2)(a), (3)(b)); deposit violations cost three times the deposit plus 5 percent interest, costs and attorney's fees (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(7)). Tenant remedies with fixed amounts: repair-and-deduct up to four months' rent in 12 months (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127L); utility or quiet-enjoyment violations, actual damages or three months' rent, whichever is greater (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14); retaliation, one to three months' rent or actual damages, whichever is greater (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 18); an unlawful lockout, three months' rent or three times the damages (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15F). A domestic-violence lock change may be charged only at the reasonable price customarily charged in the community (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 26(d)). Small claims is available for claims up to $7,000 (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 218, § 21). Massachusetts has no statewide rent-increase cap; local rent control is barred (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40P, § 4).

title: Stove and Refrigerator Duty
bodyText: Massachusetts's State Sanitary Code makes the owner provide and maintain, in each dwelling unit, a conventional cooktop and oven with at least 1.7 cubic feet of oven space and a refrigerator with freezer with at least 11.0 cubic feet of combined storage (105 CMR 410.100(A)(5)-(6)). The owner must also provide the space and proper connections for them (105 CMR 410.100(A)(4)). Both duties apply except and to the extent a written rental agreement requires the occupant to provide and maintain these items (105 CMR 410.100(A)(5)-(6)). If the written agreement shifts them to the tenant, the tenant must install and maintain the tenant-owned cooktop, oven or refrigerator free from leaks and defects (105 CMR 410.240(A)(8)-(9)). A landlord who is required by law or by the lease to furnish refrigeration service and willfully fails to do so commits an offense (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14). If you want the tenant to supply the stove or refrigerator, say so clearly in the written lease; otherwise supply both and keep them working.

title: Student Housing in Massachusetts
bodyText: Massachusetts has no licensing or certification rule for private student rentals; a privately owned apartment rented to students is an ordinary tenancy with all the usual protections. School dormitories are treated differently. Occupancy of a rooming or lodging house for three consecutive months becomes a tenancy at will, but fraternities, sororities and dormitories of educational institutions are excepted (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 17). Occupancy of a fraternity, sorority or dormitory of an educational institution, for any length of time, may be ended only by seven days' written notice from the operator (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 17). The condominium-conversion act also excludes college or school dormitories operated exclusively for educational purposes (St. 1983, c. 527, § 3). Smoking is permitted in the residential portions of a dormitory as a 'residence' under the smoke-free law (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 270, § 22(a)). If you rent to students, use a normal written lease with all co-tenants signing, and consider a guaranty for each.

title: Keeping Tenant Information Confidential
bodyText: Massachusetts has no general statute barring a landlord from sharing tenant information or setting consent rules, as Oregon's does, but several specific rules apply. An owner who obtains written proof that a tenant or household member is a victim of domestic violence, rape, sexual assault or stalking must keep it and its contents confidential and may not release it to anyone unless the victim authorizes release in writing or a court order, regulation or government audit requires it (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 24(f)). Anyone who owns or licenses personal information about a Massachusetts resident is covered by the state's data-security regulations (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93H, § 2(a)). It must give notice as soon as practicable when it knows or has reason to know of a breach (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93H, § 3(b)). Paper records with personal information must be redacted, burned, pulverized or shredded, and electronic records destroyed or erased, when disposed of (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93I, § 2). Improper disposal carries a civil fine of up to $100 per person affected, capped at $50,000 per instance (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93I, § 2). Keep applications, ID copies and bank details locked or encrypted, shred old files, and keep DV documents in a separate restricted file.

title: No Statute on Housing Your Employees
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute requiring a landlord who houses an employee (a resident manager, caretaker or farm worker) to give a disclosure of the occupancy terms, to offer a rental agreement when the job ends, or to give visitors access to employer-provided housing, as Delaware and Oregon do. The summary process statute reaches any 'lessee' or person holding under one after the lease ends, but it does not say whether an employee housed as part of the job is a tenant (Mass. Gen.
