Laws ch. 239, § 1). That question is for case law. The sanitary code covers housing and sanitation standards for farm labor camps (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 127A); those standards are in regulations on mass.gov. The cautious course: put the housing terms in a written agreement separate from the job, say what happens to the housing when employment ends, and use summary process, never a lockout, to recover the unit (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14).

title: Tenant Portals and Electronic Dealings
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute on tenant portals. Whether a landlord may require tenants to sign or pay through one turns on the electronic transactions act. That act applies only to transactions between parties who have each agreed to conduct transactions electronically, which is determined from the context and their conduct (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 110G, § 5(b)). A party who agreed to deal electronically may refuse to conduct other transactions electronically, and that right may not be waived by agreement (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 110G, § 5(c)). So a lease term requiring every future notice or signature to go through a portal can't take away a tenant's right to stop dealing electronically. No statute bars requiring rent to be paid online. A seller may not impose a surcharge on a buyer who pays by credit card (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 140D, § 28A(a)(2)); whether that reaches rent is for case law, so don't add a card surcharge. A portal or processing fee can't be required at or before move-in (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)). Offer at least one free, non-electronic way to pay rent and give notices.

title: Tenants' Right to Organize
bodyText: Massachusetts protects tenant organizing through its anti-retaliation laws. A landlord who threatens or takes reprisals against a tenant for organizing or joining a tenants' union or similar organization is liable for damages of at least one month's and up to three months' rent, or actual damages if greater, plus costs and attorney's fees (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 18). A notice of termination (other than for nonpayment), a rent increase or a substantial change in terms within six months after the tenant organized or joined such a union creates a rebuttable presumption of reprisal, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 18). Retaliation for organizing is also a defense to an eviction, with the same six-month presumption (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239, § 2A). A lease waiver of these protections is void (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 18). No statewide statute gives tenants a separate right to meet, canvass or distribute literature in a private building. Don't change a tenant's terms within six months after organizing activity unless you can document an independent reason you would have acted on anyway.

title: State-Required Statements to Tenants
bodyText: Massachusetts has no state-agency statement of tenant rights that must be attached to every lease with a signed acknowledgment, and no rule barring suit until one is given. The statements the General Laws do require are event-specific. With a security deposit, the landlord must give a statement of condition headed, in 12-point bold type, by the statutory notice explaining the tenant's right to correct it within 15 days (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(2)(c)). Before a tenancy begins, the owner must give the state lead notification materials with a tenant certification, which may be built into the lease (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, § 197A(d)(2)). With a notice to quit for nonpayment, the landlord must include the state housing office's form, which must prominently say the notice is not an eviction (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 31(a)). The court will not accept a nonpayment eviction without proof that form was delivered (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 31(b)). The sanitary code's notice of occupants' rights and responsibilities is in regulations on mass.gov.

title: No Rent-Cap or Purchase-Right Exemption Notice
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statewide rent-cap or just-cause law, and no general tenant right to purchase a building, so there is no notice telling tenants a unit is exempt from one. Cities and towns may not enact or enforce rent control except under chapter 40P's narrow voluntary terms (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40P, § 4). Publicly assisted housing whose affordability restrictions are ending has its own notice rules: the owner must give written notice to all tenants and any tenant organization, among others, at least 2 years before the restriction ends (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40T, § 2(a)). Condominium conversions of buildings with four or more units carry a notice and purchase right (St. 1983, c. 527, § 4). For ordinary private rentals, no exemption notice is needed.

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property
bodyText: Massachusetts' trespass statute lets a landlord bar a non-tenant from the property. Whoever, without right, enters or remains in or on the dwelling house, buildings or improved or enclosed land of another after being forbidden to do so by the person who has lawful control of the premises, directly or by posted notice, may be fined up to $100 or jailed up to 30 days (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 266, § 120). A person found committing the trespass may be arrested by a police officer or other listed officer (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 266, § 120). The statute does not apply to tenants or occupants who rightfully entered at the start of their tenancy and stay after it ends or is said to have ended; the landlord may recover possession from them only through civil proceedings (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 266, § 120). Whether a tenant's invited guest can be banned from the tenant's own unit, or from common areas the tenant has a right to use, is for case law. Give a ban in writing, keep a copy, and limit it to people with no tenancy of their own.

title: No Truth in Renting Act
bodyText: Massachusetts has no Truth in Renting Act like New Jersey's or Michigan's, and no required statement of the provisions a lease may not contain. Instead, specific statutes void specific lease terms, such as exculpatory clauses (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15), waivers of notices to quit (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15A), terms that conflict with the deposit statute (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(8)), jury-trial waivers (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15F) and terms ending a tenancy because a tenant has children (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 16). Leaving those terms out of your lease is the Massachusetts equivalent of a truth-in-renting check.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Massachusetts has no statute requiring parking to be rented separately from the unit, as California's unbundled-parking rule does for some new buildings, and none barring it. Any up-front parking charge or deposit at or before move-in is barred by the up-front payment limit (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b)). A monthly parking charge stated in the lease is not limited by statute. Some cities set parking requirements by zoning.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant (No Usufruct in Massachusetts)
bodyText: Massachusetts is a common-law state and has no usufruct, the civil-law right Louisiana uses. The nearest equivalent is a life estate. No Massachusetts statute says what happens to a residential lease granted by a life tenant when the life tenant dies, or requires the life tenant to disclose that status. The partition statute recognizes life tenants as holders of an interest in land (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 241, § 1), but the effect of the life tenant's death on a tenant's lease is for case law. The cautious course: if you hold only a life estate, tell the tenant in writing, and get the remainder holders to sign the lease if it may run past your lifetime.

title: Shutoff Notices to the Landlord
bodyText: Massachusetts has no rule letting a landlord, or a tenant who is the utility customer, arrange for the landlord to get copies of the tenant's shutoff notices. The utility statutes in chapter 164 address the reverse case, notice to tenants when the landlord is the customer (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, § 124D), and the Department of Public Utilities' billing and termination rules have no such provision for ordinary customers. The only third-party notice service is for customers 65 or older: if such a customer wants, the utility must send a person the customer designates notice of past-due bills, termination notices and notices of the right to a hearing, and that person is not liable for the account (220 CMR 25.05(2)). A tenant 65 or older could choose to name you, but it is the tenant's choice and you can't require it in the lease. If you need to know about a pending shutoff, the cautious course is to keep in your own name any utility whose shutoff would put the building at risk, such as heat in winter; Massachusetts limits how a landlord may charge tenants for utilities, so read the utility rows for Massachusetts before billing.

title: When Utilities Are in the Landlord's Name
bodyText: If you hold the gas or electric account for a building and fall behind, Massachusetts protects your tenants. The company may not shut off service to a tenant who is not the customer of record without giving each affected tenant notice stating the amount due, the shutoff date (15 to 30 days after the notice, as the Department of Public Utilities sets), the notice date, and the tenants' right to pay and recover the payment from the person they pay rent to (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, § 124D). Utility staff may enter common hallways to give that notice (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, § 124D). A tenant who pays may deduct the amount from rent or get reimbursement from the person last paid rent (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, § 124D). Water service has the same rules (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 165, § 11E). A lease waiver of either section is void, and reprisals against a tenant who uses these rights trigger the retaliation statutes (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, § 124D; Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 165, § 11E). A landlord required by law or the lease to furnish heat, light, power or gas who willfully fails to do so faces criminal penalties and damages of at least three months' rent (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 14). Keep utility accounts you hold current; a shutoff notice to tenants can quickly become rent deductions and a damages claim.
